comp-g01-u01.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 1 of Year 1 Computing at Ehel Academy. This is the very first unit of our youngest year, and it is called “Computers are everywhere.” It is a warm, gentle start — no test, no reading task, and no computer needed in the room. It is about noticing something wonderful: computers are all around us, and you already use them every day.

There are four big ideas, taken one at a time. First, computers are everywhere, and come in different shapes and sizes — a big desktop, a laptop that folds up, a flat tablet you touch, and a small smartphone. Second, we use computers for lots of different jobs — for fun, to make things, to talk to people far away, and to find things out. Third, computers use programs (also called apps), and different programs do different jobs. Fourth, we put things into a computer using input devices like a mouse, a keyboard, a microphone and a camera.
outcomes: Know that computers are everywhere — all around us, at home, at school and out in the world.
Recognise different types of computers — desktop, laptop, tablet and smartphone — and say which are big and which are small and easy to carry.
Know that we use computers for different things: for fun, to make things, to talk or message, and to find out things.
Know that computers use programs (also called apps), and that different programs do different jobs.
Know about input devices (mouse, keyboard, microphone, camera) and that we use them to put data — numbers, words, pictures, sounds and video — into a computer.

concept-1-computers-are-everywhere.explanation:
A computer is a clever machine that helps us do things. Computers are all around us — at home, at school, in the shop, in the car, even in a watch. We use them every single day.

What is this? Yes! And here is a secret — this is a computer.

concept-2-different-kinds-of-computers.explanation:
Computers come in different shapes and sizes. A desktop is big and stays on a desk. A laptop folds up like a book, so you can carry it. A tablet is flat and you touch it with your finger. A smartphone is small and fits in your pocket. Some computers are big, and some are small and easy to carry.

This big one stays on the desk — a desktop. This one folds up and you carry it — a laptop.
concept-2-different-kinds-of-computers.example: This flat one you touch with your finger — a tablet. And this tiny one fits in your pocket — a smartphone.

concept-3-what-do-we-use-computers-for.explanation:
We use computers for lots of different jobs. For fun — we play games, listen to music and watch videos. To make things — we draw and paint pictures. To talk or message — we video-call and chat with family and friends. To find out things — we search for answers about anything we wonder about.

What do you like to do on a phone or a tablet? Playing a game — that is for fun!
concept-3-what-do-we-use-computers-for.example: Drawing a picture — that is to make things! Calling your uncle — that is to talk!

concept-4-programs-and-apps.explanation:
A computer uses programs to do all those different jobs. Another name for a program is an app. A program tells the computer what to do. Different programs do different jobs — one program to draw, one to play a game, one to watch videos, one to make a video call.

Each of these little pictures is an app — and an app is a program. This one plays games. This one lets us draw. Different programs do different jobs.
concept-4-programs-and-apps.checkYourself: Can you understand that different programs do different jobs — a drawing app draws, a game app plays a game?

concept-5-putting-things-in-input-device.explanation:
We put things into a computer using input devices. A mouse points and chooses things on the screen. A keyboard types letters and numbers. A microphone hears your voice. A camera takes pictures and video. The things we put in — numbers, words, pictures, sounds and video — are called data.

How do I tell the computer the letter A? With the keyboard! How does it hear me sing? With the microphone! How does it take my photo? With the camera!

comp-g01-u02.unitOverview: There are three small ideas that build on each other. First, an algorithm is a set of steps in the right order — and the order matters. Second, we can follow the steps one after another, from start to finish. Third, an algorithm can be turned into code — the special language that tells a computer what to do — and a set of code that does a job is a program. So they become animators.
outcomes: Know what an algorithm is — a set of steps for a job, in the right order.
Follow the steps in an algorithm, one after another.
Know that an algorithm can be turned into code (a program the computer follows).
Join blocks in ScratchJr to make a character move.

concept-2-follow-the-steps-in-order.example: Clap 2 times, in that order. Can you invent your own two-step order for someone at home to copy?

concept-3-code-and-programs.explanation:
Computers follow steps too! The steps we give a computer are written in code. Code is the special language that tells a computer what to do. A set of code that does a job is called a program. We plan a program by first writing the algorithm — the steps — and then turning each step into a block of code.

You can be the robot yourself: give yourself an exact instruction, like “take 2 steps forward, now stop” — and only move on that exact instruction. A robot can only do exactly what it is told; it cannot guess. Now try a fuzzy command like “go over there” — you will not know what to do, because it is not exact.

comp-g01-u03.unitOverview:
The big word for the unit is data. It sounds hard, but it is simple: data is information — numbers, words, pictures or sounds. When Leila counts the mangoes in the bowl, that is data. When Leo sorts his blocks into a red pile and a blue pile, he is being a data detective.

A computing device is a machine that works with data, and it can answer our questions (a phone tells us the weather, a watch counts our steps).
outcomes: Say that data is information — numbers, words, pictures or sounds.
Say that a computing device works with data and can answer questions, and name one (a phone, a tablet, a watch).
Sort real things into groups that are the same in some way (by colour, size or kind).
Count how many things are in each group.
Colour a tiny block graph to show how many — one block for each thing.
Organise things by putting them in order (small to big, or 1, 2, 3).

concept-1-data-is-all-around-us.explanation:
Data is a fancy word for information. Data can be numbers, words, pictures or sounds. A computing device — like a phone, a tablet or a watch — is a machine that works with data. The best part: a computing device can answer our questions.

This is a computing device. It is full of data — pictures, sounds, numbers. And it can answer our questions! Watch. What is the weather today?
concept-1-data-is-all-around-us.example: See — it gave us an answer. That answer is data too.

concept-2-sorting-into-groups.explanation: To sort means to put things into groups. Things in the same group are the same in some way. We can sort by colour (all the red ones together), by size (all the big ones together), or by kind (all the animals together, all the fruit together). Tip out a basket of objects in front of you. Oh dear, all mixed up! Let us sort them — all the same-colour ones together. This is a group. Every one is red.
concept-2-sorting-into-groups.checkYourself: Can you say what makes a group the same — like colour or size? Can you make a group where everything is the same in some way?

concept-3-count-each-group-and-make-a-bl.explanation:
Once we have sorted things into groups, we can count each group to see how many. When we colour one block for each thing, we make a little picture of our data. This picture is called a block graph. A block graph makes it very easy to see which group has the most and which has the fewest.

Go back to your sorted groups from Session 2. 1, 2, 3, 4 — four red ones. Now show you the magic. Let us make a picture of this. For every red one, I colour one block. Watch. Now we can SEE it.

concept-4-putting-things-in-order.explanation: To organise data means to put it in order. We can put things in order by size — from the smallest to the biggest. We can put numbers in order — 1, 2, 3, 4. When data is in a good order, it is much easier to read. Muddle them up and ask: “Who is tallest? It is hard to tell.” Now line them up shortest to tallest: “Now it is easy! We put them in order by size.”
concept-4-putting-things-in-order.example: Try it with three objects — a small stone, a bigger one, and the biggest. If you have toys or family members of different heights nearby, line them up shortest to tallest.

concept-5-be-a-data-detective-class-surv.explanation:
A data detective asks a question, collects the answers (the data), sorts and counts each group, shows you on a block graph, and reads the graph to find the answer. This session runs the Mini-Project, “Our Favourite Fruit”.

Detectives, here is our question: which fruit does our class like best — mango, banana or apple? Let us find out with data! We are collecting our data.

comp-g01-u04.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4 of Year 1 Computing at Ehel Academy. The unit is called “Be a Designer”, but do not be fooled by the name — this is not a painting or drawing unit. It is a gentle first taste of coding. The big idea underneath the fun title is one simple sentence: when we change the steps, we change what happens. There are three small ideas in this unit, and they build on each other. First, a character can move in three ways we can change — how fast it goes (its speed), how far it goes (the number of steps), and which way it goes (the direction). Second, and most important, changing the steps changes the outcome: the word outcome simply means “what happens” or “the result”. Third, we can guess (predict) what a program will do just by looking at its blocks, and then run it to check if we were right.

concept-1-steps-in-order-what-is-an-algo.explanation:
An algorithm is a set of steps for doing a job, and the steps must be in the right order. We follow algorithms every day without knowing the word.

When we wash our hands, we do the steps in order — we do not dry our hands before we wash them! Steps in the right order are called an algorithm. It is a big word for a simple thing.

concept-2-change-the-steps-change-what-h.explanation:
This is the heart of the unit. If we change a step, we change the outcome — the outcome just means “what happens”. A moving character can be changed in three ways: how fast (speed), how far (the number of steps), and which way (the direction).

Everyone stands on a start line. Do it with your bodies on the floor. Give a step, then change it, and you can feel the difference.

concept-3-turning-steps-into-blocks-meet.explanation:
An algorithm can become a program — steps a tablet can follow. In ScratchJr we do not write words; we join coloured picture blocks. Each block is one step. We can read the blocks to know what the character will do.

First, unplugged, lay out your big paper blocks in a row and “read” them like a story. Teach the colours as a little song, because a child can find a block by its colour long before they can read it

concept-4-change-a-block-change-the-outc.explanation:
Now we put Session 2 and Session 3 together. When we change a block in our program, the outcome changes — just like changing a step on the floor. And before we run it, we can predict: look at the blocks and guess what will happen.

Go back to the Rabbit program from last time. Let us make the Rabbit FAST.

comp-g01-u05.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 5 of Year 1 Computing at Ehel Academy. This is a warm, gentle unit about networks. A network is what we make when we join two or more computers or devices together so they can talk to each other and share. You already live with networks every day, even without the word for it: the tablet a mother uses to video-call family in Hargeisa, and the little box on the wall that gives the whole home its Wi-Fi, are both part of networks.

First, that a network is two or more computers or devices joined together. Second, that a network lets us communicate (send a message to a friend) and share (a photo, or one printer between many computers). Third, that many devices can join — a laptop, tablet, phone, smartwatch or printer — but some things cannot, such as a bicycle. Last, you meet the internet: the biggest network in the whole world, where we can chat with friends, share pictures and play games.
outcomes: Say what a network is — two or more computers or devices joined together.
Know that a network lets us communicate — send a message to a friend.
Know that a network lets us share — such as a photo, or one printer used by many computers.
Name some devices that can join a network (a laptop, a tablet, a phone, a smartwatch, a printer), and know that some things (like a bicycle) cannot join.
Say what the internet is — the biggest network in the whole world — and that we can chat, share pictures and play games on it.

concept-1-what-is-a-network-we-join-toge.explanation:
A network is when we join two or more computers or devices together. One device all on its own cannot share with anyone. But when we join devices together, they can talk to each other and share.

Here is one tablet, all by itself. It is lonely — it cannot send a message to anyone. But watch. Now they are joined together.

concept-2-which-things-can-join-a-networ.explanation:
Lots of devices can join a network — a laptop, a tablet, a phone, a smartwatch and a printer. But not everything can join. A bicycle, a ball or a chair cannot join a network — they are not devices that connect.

Introduce the devices one at a time, with a picture or a mime, each in one friendly sentence

concept-3-what-a-network-lets-us-do-talk.explanation:
A network lets us do two lovely things. It lets us communicate — send a message to a friend. And it lets us share — share a photo with someone, or share one printer between many computers so everyone can use it.

Go back to the human network from Session 1. When you passed the Hello note around the circle, you were communicating — sending a message. Networks let computers do the very same thing.
concept-3-what-a-network-lets-us-do-talk.checkYourself: Can you remember that a device must be joined before it can share? Can you name one thing a network lets us do — send a message, share a photo, or share a printer?

concept-4-the-internet-the-biggest-netwo.explanation:
The internet is the biggest network in the whole world. It joins computers and devices all around the world, not just in one room. On the internet we can chat with friends, share pictures, and play games with friends far away.

In our human network game, we joined a few children in one room. Now imagine a network so big that it joins every country — phones in Hargeisa, tablets in Mogadishu, computers in London, all joined together. That giant network is the internet.

concept-5-make-a-network-our-playdough-p.explanation:
This session pulls the whole unit together. There is nothing new to learn — it is a happy chance to use every word from the unit: network, connect, communicate, device, share, internet.

Today you are the network builders! With your partner, make devices out of playdough — maybe a tablet, a phone and a printer — then join them together to make a network.

comp-g01-u06.unitOverview:
The big idea of this unit is simple and joyful: when something goes wrong, we can find the mistake and fix it. That is what it means to be a problem solver. First, you learn to put steps in the right order — because a list of steps only works if the steps come in the right order (you cannot cook the anjero before you mix it). Second, you learn to find a wrong step in a list — a step that points the wrong way or has the wrong number. Third, you meet the computer word for a mistake in a program: a bug. Finding and fixing a bug is called debugging, and it is a normal, happy part of the work.

A list of steps in the right order has a special name: an algorithm. a list of steps. You only need to feel it: the steps to make anjero, the steps to walk to the park, the steps to get ready for school. Every one of these is an algorithm.
outcomes: Put a short list of instructions (2-4 steps) into the right order.
Say, in their own words, why the order matters — for example, you cannot cook the anjero before you mix it.
Understand that a list of steps in the right order is called an algorithm (a list of steps).
Find the wrong step in a short algorithm — a step that goes the wrong way or has the wrong number.

comp-g01-u07.unitOverview:
The big idea of this unit is a lovely surprise: computers are not only the big screen on a desk or the tablet in your hand — tiny computers hide inside all sorts of everyday things, and they are the boss. A washing machine, a microwave, a fridge and even some toys have a little computer inside. We cannot see it, but it is there, and it controls the machine — it tells the machine what to do. The word for that is control, and it is the heart of the whole unit.

First, that some everyday devices use computers — and what each hidden computer controls (the fridge computer keeps our food cold, the microwave computer sets the cooking time). Second, what a robot is — a machine with a computer inside that can do a job all by itself, with no person helping. You learn the happy, important truth that a robot is a machine, not a person: it cannot feel sad or happy. Third, that computers give us information back, called output — and the output devices that show it to us: a speaker to hear, a screen to see, a printer to put words and pictures on paper.
outcomes: Know that some everyday devices have a computer inside them (a washing machine, a microwave, a fridge, some toys).
Say that the computer controls the device — it tells it what to do — and give one example ("the fridge computer keeps our food cold").
Sort simple things into has a computer and no computer.
Say what a robot is: a machine that does a job by itself, with no help from a person.
Know that a robot is not alive and cannot feel happy or sad.
Name one place a robot works (a factory, a dangerous job, or a place people cannot go, like Mars).
Know that a robot that looks like a person is called an android.
Know that computers give us output, and match an output device to its job (a speaker to hear, a screen to see, a printer to put on paper).

comp-g01-u08.unitOverview:
The big idea of this unit is joyful and very hands-on: we can find things out, write them down, and then look at what we found. That is what it means to be a data collector. Nadia likes mango. Six children walked to school. When we ask a question and gather everyone's answers, we are collecting data.

First, you learn to record data using a form — a form is just a list of questions, and we write our answer next to each question. Forms can be on paper, or on a computer (an electronic form). Second, you learn to sort and group the data — put the same answers together — and to count each group, using tally marks and then a pictogram (a picture chart where one coloured box stands for one thing). Third, you learn to answer questions using what they made: How many? Which is the most (the favourite)? Which has the fewest?

Record data by filling in a simple form (a list of questions), and know that a form can be on paper or on a computer.
Sort a small set of answers into groups (put the same ones together).
Count each group and use tally marks (one mark for one thing).
Make a simple pictogram by colouring one box for each thing.
Read a pictogram or a data table to answer questions — how many, which is the most (the favourite), and which has the fewest.
Enjoy being a data collector and take pride in the chart they made.

comp-g01-u09.unitOverview:
The big idea of this unit is joyful: we can make our own little games, and then we try them to see if they work. But the real computing lesson is not “make a big game”. It is three tiny skills, taught one at a time, in the happy context of making games. Second, you learn to find an error — to spot where the blocks do not match their plan. Third, you learn to debug — to fix the wrong block so the game works. These three skills are the whole unit.

The star word of this unit is testing — simply trying your program to see if it works. If it does what we wanted, it works. If it does the wrong thing, we have found an error, and fixing that error is called debugging. Mistakes are completely normal — even the grown-ups who make the biggest games test them over and over to find and fix errors.
outcomes: Say what a games developer is — a person who makes computer games — and feel like one.
In ScratchJr, add a character and join a few picture blocks to make a tiny game.
Use the Start on Tap block so the character does something when it is tapped.
Run and test a program — try it (for a tap game, tap the character) and check it does what they wanted.
Understand that testing means trying your program to see if it works.
Predict what a short program will do, then test it to find out.
Find an error — spot the one block that does not match the plan (a wrong number, direction, or start block).
Know that fixing an error is called debugging, and debug a short program by changing one block and testing again.
Stay cheerful about mistakes and keep trying — the heart of being a games developer.

A games developer is a person who makes computer games. Today we become games developers. A game has a character (like a frog) and blocks that tell it what to do. Some games do something when you tap them.

Who has played a game on a tablet or a phone? What did you do — did you tap the screen? Did you make something jump? The people who make those games have a special name. They are called games developers.

outcomes: Say that two or more computers joined together is called a network.
Know that other devices, not only computers, can join a network too (like a printer or a tablet).
Say that connected computers can share — they can talk to each other and share pictures and words.
Name devices that connect with wires — for example a printer, a desktop computer or a games console.
Name devices that connect without wires — for example a smartphone, a tablet, a laptop or a camera.
Know that the internet is lots and lots of computers joined together all around the world.
Know that when a device is joined to the internet we are online, and we can share pictures, video-call and watch videos.
Know that sometimes there is no internet (we are offline), and then some things — like an online video — will not work.

concept-1-what-is-a-network.explanation: One computer on its own is just one computer. When two or more computers are joined together, we call it a network. When they are joined, they can share — they can talk to each other and share pictures and words. Other devices, like a printer, can join too. Here is one computer, and here is another computer. On their own, they cannot share. Now they are joined. They are connected. Two or more computers joined together is a network! Look — they can share!
concept-1-what-is-a-network.example: Act it out with your own bodies. Ask a friend or family member to stand apart from you.

concept-2-connect-with-a-wire.explanation:
Some computers and devices join a network with a wire. A wire is a cord that carries the sharing from one device to another. Things that often use a wire are a desktop computer, a printer and a games console.

This is a wire. A wire joins two devices so they can share. Can the computer send its picture to the printer to print? Not yet — they are not joined.

concept-3-connect-without-a-wire.example: A phone can join with no wire — that is why you can watch it in the park or on a bus, far from any cord. Some clever devices, like a laptop or a tablet, can join either way — with a wire or without one!

concept-4-the-internet-computers-all-aro.explanation:
The internet is the biggest network of all. It is lots and lots of computers joined together all around the world. When your device joins the internet, you can reach people and things very, very far away — you can video-call family, share photos, and watch videos.

Dot lots of little computers all around it and join them with lines. All these computers, all around the world, are joined together. That giant network is the internet. Imani lives here.

comp-g01-u11.unitOverview:
The big idea is joyful and simple: we can be artists by giving directions. An artist draws a picture. It is just like telling a friend, “go right, now down, now left, now up,” until a shape appears. This is the very first taste of how computers and drawing robots make pictures.

First, they give and follow directions — the four arrows up, down, left and right. They play the arrows with their whole bodies, follow arrows across a floor grid to reach a friend, and put the steps in the right order. Second, they give instructions for a simple task — a short list of steps (an algorithm) that draws a shape or walks a character along a path.
outcomes: Name and show the four directions with arrows: up, down, left and right.
Follow a short list of arrow steps to move along a path and reach a target (for example, help Maya reach the garden).
Give simple directions to move something from one square to another.
Understand that a short list of steps in the right order is an algorithm (a list of instructions), and that it needs a start and a stop.
Put a few direction steps into the right order to match a path.
Draw a shape — a square or a rectangle — by following a list of direction steps (be an artist!).
In ScratchJr, add a character and join Move blocks so it walks to a target, then tap the green flag to run it.
Find and fix a wrong step in a short set of directions, and keep trying cheerfully.

comp-g02-u01.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 1 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy. The unit is called “Be a Game Developer”, but the big idea underneath the fun title is two words: algorithms and programs. An algorithm is a set of clear, step-by-step instructions, in the right order, for doing a job. A program is a set of instructions that a computer can follow.

Getting dressed, tidying their toys, or helping to make anjero are all algorithms — steps done in the right order. We start from these everyday steps and slowly give you the computing words for what they already do.

There are three big ideas in this unit. First, an algorithm must be precise — that means exact, clear and correct. “Move” is not precise; “Move 4 steps forward” is precise. Second, programs tell computers what to do, and a computer follows the steps exactly because a computer cannot think for itself. Third, we can turn an algorithm into a program by changing each step into a block of code, and then run it.

concept-1-what-is-an-algorithm-giving-cl.explanation:
An algorithm is a set of steps for doing a job. For the steps to work, each instruction must be clear — it must say exactly what to do. A fuzzy instruction like “Move” leaves you guessing; a clear one like “Take 4 steps forward” does not.

Simon says take 4 steps forward. Simon says move. Why did everyone do something different when I just said 'move'? Because 'move' does not tell us enough!

A computer is a machine — it cannot think for itself, so it does exactly what the program says, no more and no less. That is why the instructions in a program must be precise. The robot may only do exactly what it is told. Robot, take 3 steps forward. Now turn right. Now stop. Now go over there.

comp-g02-u02.unitOverview: There are four big ideas in the unit. First, data means the facts we collect — and data can be words (like favourite fruit) as well as numbers. We can sort data into groups, also called categories. Second, we count our data, and a tally (a little mark for each thing) helps us count without losing our place. Third, we can present our data — show it — as a pictogram (a chart made of pictures) or a bar graph, sometimes called a block graph (a chart made of bars or blocks).

concept-1-what-is-data-sorting-into-grou.checkYourself: Can you suggest a second, different way to group the same things? Can you place each item in the correct group?

concept-2-counting-data-with-a-tally.explanation:
Once our data is in groups, we want to know how many are in each group. We count. A tally is a little mark we make — one mark for each thing — so we do not lose our place while counting. At the end we count the marks and write the total in a table.

Let us find out our favourite fruit. When I point to you, tell me: mango, banana or dates. Now we count the marks.

concept-3-showing-data-with-pictures-pic.explanation:
After we count, we present the data — we show it so it is easy to read. One way is a pictogram. A pictogram uses pictures, and each picture stands for one thing. A little note called a key tells us what one picture means. The longest row has the most; the shortest row has the least.

Make a real pictogram on the wall. Have them stick their card in the right row, all lined up neatly starting from the same edge.
concept-3-showing-data-with-pictures-pic.example: Then count together to check. Give you a sticky note or card and ask how they came to Ehel Academy today — walk, car or bus.

concept-4-showing-data-with-blocks-bar-g.explanation: Another way to present data is a bar graph, also called a block graph. Instead of pictures, we colour blocks — one block for each thing, with no gaps between them. The tallest or longest bar shows the most. A bar graph shows the SAME data as a pictogram, just in a different way. We can make a bar graph by hand, or a computer can make one for us in seconds. Go back to the fruit tally from “Counting data with a tally” (mango 4, banana 2, dates 1). One block for each child. No gaps — the blocks touch.

concept-5-why-computers-store-data-and-c.explanation:
Computers are very good at keeping — storing — lots of data. There are two ideas here. First, storing data on a computer is helpful because a computer can keep a huge amount, find it fast, show it as charts, share it with other computers, change it easily, and make a copy. A copy kept safe, in case the first one is lost, is called a backup. Second, data is collected all around us for a reason — a school form asks which club you like, a shop till reads a barcode to know what was sold, and machines by the road count how much traffic goes past.

Imagine writing every child's favourite fruit in the whole school on paper — that is a huge pile, and hard to search. A computer keeps it all neatly and finds any answer in a blink.
concept-5-why-computers-store-data-and-c.example: And it keeps a spare copy, a backup, so the data is safe. When Mum buys rice, the till beeps — it is reading the barcode, those little black lines, to know what it is and how much it costs.
concept-5-why-computers-store-data-and-c.checkYourself: Can you know a backup is an extra, safe copy — not the same as deleting the first one? Can you name one place data is collected? Can you give one reason computers are good at storing data?

comp-g02-u03.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 3 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is about computers and the jobs they do. There is no coding in this unit — it is all about noticing computers around us and learning the words to talk about them.

A tablet with a story app, a phone to video-call grandmother, the laptop at Ehel Academy, a smartwatch on a wrist — these are all computers. This unit helps you notice that, and gives you simple words for the parts and the jobs.

Every computer is made of two things: hardware (the parts we can touch) and software (the instructions inside, which we cannot touch).

concept-2-hardware-the-parts-we-can-touc.explanation:
Every computer is made of hardware. Hardware is all the parts we can see and touch — the screen, the keyboard, the mouse, the headphones. Some hardware is hidden inside where we cannot see it, but it is still there.

Touch it. The glass screen, the buttons, the case — all the parts your fingers can feel — that is the hardware.

concept-3-software-the-instructions-insi.explanation:
A computer also needs software. Software is the set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do. We cannot touch software. An app is software that does one job — a drawing app, a story app, a counting game. Hardware and software work together: the hardware is the parts, and the software tells the parts what to do.

Your hands are a bit like hardware — they can do things. But your hands wait for your head to tell you what to do. Software is like those instructions.
concept-3-software-the-instructions-insi.example: When Leila taps the story app, the app is the software. It tells the tablet — the hardware — to show the page and play the story.

concept-4-putting-things-in-and-getting-.explanation: Hardware can do two different jobs. Some hardware lets us put things INTO the computer — we call these input devices (a keyboard, a mouse, a microphone, a camera). Some hardware lets the computer give things OUT for us to see or hear — these are output devices (a screen, a speaker, headphones, a printer). For input, push your hands towards yourself (“IN”). For output, push your hands away (“OUT”). When Sami types on the keyboard, he is putting letters IN. The keyboard is an input device.

comp-g02-u05.unitOverview: You learn three big ideas. First, that many different devices can connect to a network — not only computers, but also things like a smart TV, a smart light bulb, an e-reader, a scanner and a security camera. Second, that two devices can work together, and that a device joined to others can do much more than a device standing all alone. Third, you learn to say the words wired (joined with a cable you can see) and wireless (joined through the air, with no cable), and to tell the two apart. Almost everything here is unplugged — done on paper, with string and cards, or by acting things out — so no computer is needed. Acting as devices yourself, joined by string and passing a message hand to hand, teaches the idea better than any screen could.

concept-1-devices-that-can-join-a-networ.explanation:
A device is a machine like a tablet, a phone or a printer. When we join devices together so they can share and send messages, we make a network. Lots of devices — not only computers — can join a network.

You already know that tablets, laptops and phones can join a network. But guess what — many more devices can join too!

concept-2-alone-or-joined-working-togeth.explanation:
A device on its own is a standalone device. It cannot talk to any other device. When we join a device to others, it becomes a connected device — and two connected devices can do more together than one device can do alone.

Imagine you are all alone in a room with the door shut. You cannot pass a note to a friend, because there is no friend to pass it to. That is a standalone device — all by itself. Now open the door and join hands with a friend.

concept-3-wireless-networks-no-wires.explanation:
A wireless network joins devices through the air, with no cable at all. Because there is no wire holding them, the devices can move around and still stay joined. Wireless networks are popular in homes and cafes. Tablets, laptops and phones usually join wireless networks.

When you carry a tablet from the kitchen to the garden and it still works, that is a wireless network. There is no cable trailing behind you — the network reaches you through the air, a bit like sound or sunshine. That is why you can walk about and stay joined.

concept-4-wired-networks-and-telling-the.example: A desktop computer stays on its desk, joined by a cable — it does not walk around. Wired networks are strong and steady, so schools and offices like to use them.

concept-5-draw-and-sort-our-networks.explanation:
This session pulls the unit together. There is nothing new to learn — it is a happy chance to use every word from the unit: device, network, connect, share, wired, wireless.

Today you are the network builders! You will draw devices, join them together, and say whether your network is wired or wireless.

comp-g02-u06.unitOverview:
The first idea is the algorithm. An algorithm is just a set of instructions in the right order. The second idea is the program. When we write our algorithm as blocks that a computer can follow, we have made a program. The third idea is debugging. A mistake in a program is called a bug. Finding it and fixing it is called debugging — and it is much faster and more fun when we work with a friend.

The free tool for this unit is ScratchJr. The source textbook names ScratchJr directly, so we use exactly the tool it intends. This is a colourful app made especially for you aged five to seven, so it is a perfect fit for Year 2. There is no reading of code and no typing — you simply drag picture blocks together and tap the green flag to see their character move. You join blocks like Start on Green Flag, Hop, Turn Right and Move Right to bring a dancer to life.

comp-g02-u07.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 7 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy. A data scientist sounds like a very big job, but it just means you ask good questions, collect the answers (which we call data), sort the data into the right kind, and use it to help solve a problem. This unit gives simple names to clever thinking you already do. There are three big ideas, and they build on each other. The first idea is that questions come in two kinds. A statistical question has more than one answer — like “What are the favourite snacks of the children in our class?” A non-statistical question has only one answer — like “What colour is Leo’s bag?” The second idea is that the data we collect also comes in two kinds. Numerical data is numbers — things we count or measure, like height or test scores. Categorical data is groups — words like eye colour or favourite fruit. The third idea is the best part: data helps us solve problems. Almost all of this unit is unplugged — it is done on paper, with sorting cards, and with a tape measure. There is no app to download and no account to make. The one place a computer appears is the idea of an electronic form (a set of questions on a screen); you can see what a form looks like on a printed sheet, or on any tablet or phone you already have, but you never need to sign in anywhere.

concept-1-questions-one-answer-or-many-a.explanation: Questions come in two kinds. A statistical question has more than one answer — the answers can be different for different people. A non-statistical question has only one answer. Being a data scientist starts with knowing which kind of question we are asking. “What colour is my bag?” has only one answer. “What is your favourite fruit?” has lots of different answers, because everyone likes something different.

concept-2-two-kinds-of-data-numbers-and-.explanation:
When we ask a many-answer (statistical) question, we collect data. That data comes in two kinds. Numerical data is numbers — things we can count or measure, like height, test scores or how many pets. Categorical data is groups — words that sort things into kinds, like eye colour, favourite fruit or how we travel to school.

Some data is numbers we count or measure — that is numerical data. Some data is groups, like colours or names — that is categorical data.

comp-g02-u08.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy. You will not paint with a brush — instead you give a device a careful set of instructions, and the device draws a shape or walks a path shaped like a letter. When the instructions are right, a picture appears. That is the art. The first big idea is the algorithm — a set of instructions in the right order. To make a drawing, the device needs simple commands: marker down (start drawing), move forward (go straight), turn left or turn right (make a corner), and stop. If you draw the little foot of a letter L before the tall line, you get the wrong shape. The second big idea is programming a device. Some devices can move. We write instructions and the device follows them — a little robot on the floor, or a character on a screen. The clever part, and the reason this is an art unit, is that the path the device travels can make a picture or a letter. Programming a robot to walk in the shape of a C or an L is drawing with movement.

concept-1-be-the-marker-an-algorithm-tha.explanation: An algorithm is a set of instructions in the right order. To draw, a device follows commands. The most important one today is marker down — it means “put the pen on the paper and start drawing”. Then Move forward makes a line. Imagine you are a drawing robot, but you only do what you are told, one command at a time: draw a line. How far? Which way?
concept-1-be-the-marker-an-algorithm-tha.example: And my marker is still up, so nothing happens! Now you can give clear commands and follow them exactly.

concept-2-turns-make-corners-drawing-a-l.explanation: A turn makes a corner. Turn left and Turn right each turn a quarter — like turning to face the side of the room. A turn happens on the spot; it does not move you forward. By joining Move forward and turns, we can draw a whole letter. Stand up and face the front. Say “Turn right!” and make a quarter turn. Say “Turn right again!” and you are now facing the back.

concept-3-program-a-robot-on-the-floor-g.explanation: Some devices can move. We can program them by writing instructions for them to follow. And here is the art: the path can be the shape of a letter. Imagine a big grid on the floor, about four squares by four squares. A robot (or a soft toy) stands on a square and faces one way, and you program it to walk a path shaped like an L.

comp-g02-u09.unitOverview:
There are two big ideas, and both are simple. The first is knowing when the internet is here or not. Our devices show us little pictures called icons that tell us whether we are connected. When the internet is here to use, we say it is available; when it is not here, it is not available.

The second big idea is sharing safely. When devices are connected, information can travel between them — something on one device can be seen on another. That is wonderful: we can send a photo or a warm hello to family far away, from Hargeisa to Mogadishu in a moment. But because other people can see what we send, we learn to think first. They finish with five simple stay-safe rules.
outcomes: Know when a network and the internet are available (here to use) and when they are not available.
Read simple icons that show a device is connected without wires, connected with a wire, or not connected at all.
Say what you cannot do with no internet — send emails, look at websites, or watch online videos.
Understand that connected devices share information, so something on one device can be seen by another.
Understand, in a gentle way, that malware is a program that is bad for a computer, and that we do not open files from people we do not know.

concept-2-sharing-across-a-network-think.explanation: When devices are connected, they can share information. That means something on one device can be seen by another device. Sharing is wonderful — but because other people can see what we send, we learn to think first. Imagine passing a note around a circle of friends, hand to hand: could the person next to you see it? Could lots of people see it as it went around?
concept-2-sharing-across-a-network-think.example: Write or draw something small and happy on a slip of paper (a star, a fruit), then imagine it being passed hand to hand around a circle of friends.

concept-4-careful-what-we-open-malware.explanation:
Malware is a program that is bad for a computer. Some people try to trick us by sending malware across a network. We receive information when we open a website or download a file — so we do not open files, messages or links from people we do not know. A computer with malware acts strangely: it slows down, strange adverts pop up, files will not open, or it stops working.

The word malware means bad software — a naughty program. It can make a computer poorly, a bit like a germ makes us poorly. How do we stay well?
concept-4-careful-what-we-open-malware.example: We are careful. A computer stays well when we are careful too — we only open files and messages from people we know and trust, and we check with a grown-up.

concept-5-our-safety-rules-staying-safe-.explanation:
We finish by gathering everything into five simple stay-safe rules: keep your information private, only click links and downloads you trust, tell a trusted adult if something feels wrong, be kind to others online, and check with an adult before sharing photos or videos. Say each rule to yourself and picture what it means.

Try it: pick one rule and think of a real example of following it.
concept-5-our-safety-rules-staying-safe-.checkYourself: Can you say at least two of the five stay-safe rules in your own words?

concept-3-keep-your-private-things-priva.explanation:
Personal information is private information about YOU. It includes your home address, your phone number, your family’s names, your birthday, and your school’s name. The biggest risk on a network is sharing personal information, because people we do not know might see it.

“My favourite colour is green” is fine to tell everyone. “My home address is 12 Oak Street” is private, just for your family. Personal information is like the key to your house.
concept-3-keep-your-private-things-priva.example: You would not hand your house key to someone you do not know. We keep personal information private in the same way.

comp-g02-u10.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 10 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy. Instead of writing a story on paper, you bring a story to life on a screen: you choose characters and a background, make the characters talk in speech bubbles, and make them take turns so they have a proper conversation. The star of the show is the Say block, which makes a character speak. That is how a back-and-forth conversation is built. The free tool for this unit is ScratchJr, a colourful app made especially for you aged five to seven. There is no code to read and nothing to type in as commands — you simply drag picture blocks together and tap the green flag to watch your story play. To make two characters talk to each other, you use messages: one character finishes speaking and sends a coloured message, and the other character is waiting for that colour and starts speaking when it arrives. First, you learn to predict what an algorithm will do. An algorithm takes something in (the input) and gives something back out (the output), and we can work out the output ourselves by doing the steps the way the computer would. Second, you learn to test as you build — to check each character’s part works before moving on, so mistakes do not pile up. Third, you learn to debug: to find the one block that is wrong and fix it.

concept-2-make-a-character-talk-the-say-.explanation: Today we open ScratchJr and meet the Say block. The Say block makes a character speak — the words pop up in a speech bubble. This is how we tell a story on the screen. The yellow Start on Green Flag block starts everything when we tap the green flag. Tap the blue plus to add a character — this is Nadia.

concept-3-taking-turns-messages-and-test.example: Add Nadia and give her Try it with a mismatch for fun — Nadia holds up orange but Leo is only watching for red — and Leo stays silent. You instantly see: the colours must match.

concept-4-two-scenes-and-debugging-toget.explanation: A story can have more than one scene. In ScratchJr, each page is a scene. A Go to Page block turns the page to a new background. We also learn to debug: a bug is a mistake in a program, and debugging is finding the wrong block and fixing it. Set Page 2 to a new background — the date table. Add a Go to Page block at the end of Leo’s reply so the story moves on after the greeting. A project can have two pages — tap the page thumbnails on the right to see them.

concept-5-be-a-storyteller-the-mini-proj.example: First plan what you say, then build it, testing as you go — and if there is a bug, find it with your partner. Keep the story short — a greeting and one reply is a complete story.

comp-g02-u11.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 11 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy — and well done, because this is the last unit of Year 2! There is no new software to learn; instead you talk, sort, and play a game to explore three big ideas: what computers are good at, how people pick the right device, and the difference between real robots and the make-believe robots we see in films.

The first idea is that computers can do some things better than people. A computer is very fast, it never gets tired or bored, it can store a whole library of books inside one small machine, and it follows instructions exactly.

The second idea is that people choose different computer devices for different reasons. A desktop is powerful with a large screen, but heavy; a laptop, a tablet and a smartphone are smaller and easy to carry. The best device depends on what you need it for and where you are.
outcomes: Name some tasks computers can do better than people — work fast, never get tired or bored, store a lot, and follow instructions exactly.
Understand that people are still better at some things, like making up something new (a story, a picture, a joke).
Know that people use different computer devices — desktop, laptop, tablet and smartphone.
Give a simple reason for choosing a device (for example, "a tablet is light and easy to carry").
Say what a robot is — a machine that does a task without help from a person.
Tell the difference between a real robot and a fictional (make-believe) robot.
Give the robot a short, correct sequence of steps to reach a place, and understand a robot does exactly what it is told.
Find and fix a wrong step in a short set of robot instructions.

concept-1-what-computers-can-do-better-t.explanation:
Computers can do some things better than people. A computer is very fast, it never gets tired or bored, it can store a huge amount in a small space, and it follows instructions exactly. But people are still better at some things, like making up something brand new.

comp-g03-u01.unitOverview: First, you learn to follow an algorithm (do the steps one by one) and understand it (say what job it does). Second, you learn to edit and correct an algorithm when a step is wrong or out of order. Third, you learn that the best algorithms are efficient and concise — they do the job in the fewest steps — and you learn to make instructions shorter by combining steps that repeat. Fourth, they move onto the computer and learn to make a simple Scratch program more concise, and to reset a character back to where it started.
outcomes: Follow and understand an algorithm, and say what job it does.
Edit and correct an algorithm that has a wrong step or steps in the wrong order.
Understand that an efficient algorithm is concise — it uses the fewest steps.
Make instructions shorter by combining repeated steps and removing steps that are not needed.
In Scratch, build a short program and make it more concise.
In Scratch, add blocks to reset a sprite's position and size so a program can be run again and again.

concept-3-making-it-concise-combining-re.explanation:
The best algorithms are efficient — they do the job in the fewest steps. A short algorithm is concise. One easy way to make an algorithm concise is to look for steps that repeat, and combine them into one step.

Do what I say: clap, clap, clap. That was three steps. Is there a shorter way to say it?

concept-5-resetting-objects-in-scratch.explanation:
In many games, a character goes back to the start after each go. We call this a reset. In Scratch, a program does not reset by itself. If we make a sprite move up or grow bigger, and then run the program again, it carries on from where it stopped — it floats off the top or grows too big. To fix this, we add blocks that put the sprite back to its starting position and size.

Think of a board game. After each go, you put the counter back on Start so you can play again.

concept-4-concise-programs-in-scratch.explanation:
The same idea works on the computer. In Scratch we join coloured blocks to make a program. If the same block repeats, we can often combine them into one block. This makes the program more concise.

comp-g03-u02.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 2 of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is all about the two parts that make every computer work: hardware and software. Hardware is the name for all the parts you can touch — the screen, the keyboard, the mouse. Software is the set of instructions, also called apps, that tell the hardware what to do. The big idea of the whole unit is simple: hardware and software must work together. One without the other does nothing.

First, you learn what hardware and software are, and why a computer needs both. Second, you learn that hardware comes in three groups — input devices (that put information in), output devices (that show us the result), and storage devices (that keep our files). Third, you learn that input devices can be manual (a person works them, like a keyboard) or automatic (they work with little or no help, like a fire alarm sensor).
outcomes: Say what hardware is (the physical parts you can touch) and give examples.
Say what software is (the instructions, or apps, that tell the hardware what to do) and give examples.
Explain why a computer needs both hardware and software to work.
Name the three categories of hardware — input, output and storage — and sort devices into them.
Describe some ways hardware and software are different (touch, damage, bugs).
Tell the difference between a manual and an automatic input device, and name examples of each.

concept-1-what-are-hardware-and-software.explanation:
A computer is made of two things that work together. Hardware is all the parts you can touch. Software is the set of instructions — also called apps — that tell the hardware what to do. A computer needs both. Without software, the hardware does not know what to do; without hardware, the software has nowhere to run.

Everything I can touch — the screen, the buttons, the glass — is the hardware. But on its own it is just plastic and glass.

concept-2-three-kinds-of-hardware-input-.explanation:
Hardware comes in three groups. Input devices put information IN (a keyboard, a mouse, a microphone). Output devices show the result OUT to us (a screen, a speaker, a printer). Storage devices keep our files to use later (a USB drive, a hard drive).

Your eyes and ears take things IN — they are like input. Your mouth talks OUT — that is like output. Your memory keeps things to use later — that is like storage.

concept-4-manual-and-automatic-input-dev.explanation:
There are two kinds of input devices. A manual input device needs a person to work it — you move the mouse with your hand, you press the keys with your fingers. An automatic input device works with little or no help from a person. Automatic devices are often more accurate, because a person can make mistakes when typing.

Watch me type. I have to press every single key with my fingers. That is manual — it needs me. Now think about the fire alarm on the ceiling. Nobody presses it.

comp-g03-u03.unitOverview: First, you learn that data helps us solve problems — we collect the data, look at it carefully, understand what it tells us, and then make a good decision. Second, you learn that data comes in different kinds — categorical data is groups of words (like favourite fruit), and discrete data is whole numbers we count (like how many pets a family has). Third, you learn to organise and present data as a tally chart, a pictogram, and a block or column chart, and to read a chart to answer questions. Fourth, you learn how data is recorded on computers using input devices and electronic forms, and you make one simple chart on screen.

concept-1-data-helps-us-solve-problems.explanation:
Data is the facts and numbers we collect. Data helps us solve problems and make good choices. There are three steps: first we collect the data, then we look at it carefully, then we understand what it is telling us. After that, we can make a good decision.

When we want to solve a problem, we do not just guess. We collect some facts — that is data. Then we look at the data and think about what it means.

concept-2-two-kinds-of-data-categorical-.explanation:

comp-g03-u04.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4 of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. The word “designer” here does not mean drawing pictures; it means planning what a program should do, choosing the steps, and putting them in the best order. It carries straight on from Unit 1, where you first met algorithms (step-by-step instructions for doing a job). First, you learn that different algorithms can solve the same problem, and the best one is efficient — it does the job in the fewest steps. A short algorithm is concise. Second, you learn to spot steps that repeat in everyday tasks, so those steps can be said once instead of many times. Third, you learn to run two algorithms at the same time in Scratch, and see how they can affect each other. Fourth, you learn to reset the characters back to their starting places so the program can be run again and again.

concept-1-efficient-algorithms-the-fewes.explanation:
Different algorithms can solve the same problem. The best one is efficient — it reaches the goal in the fewest steps. A short algorithm is concise.

This frog wants to reach the pond. There is more than one way to write the steps. Draw a little frog on one side of the board and a pond on the other.

concept-2-spotting-steps-that-repeat.explanation:
A repetitive task has actions that are done more than once. Instead of writing the same step over and over, we can write it once and say “repeat”. Finding the repeat is another way to make an algorithm concise.

Talk about riding a bicycle. To keep the bicycle moving you push down with your left foot, then your right foot, then left, then right — over and over.

concept-5-reset-the-objects.checkYourself: Can you use negative numbers in the go to x: y: block to put a sprite back to a starting place on the left or below the middle? Do you run the program more than once to test the reset?

concept-3-into-scratch-build-it-and-make.explanation:
The same ideas work on the computer. In Scratch we join coloured blocks to build a program. If the same block repeats, we can often combine them into one block to make the program more concise.

Delete the cat by clicking the little bin on its picture, then add the Ball sprite and a simple backdrop like Blue Sky. Open Scratch at scratch.mit.edu and click Create.

comp-g03-u05.unitOverview: First, you learn what a network is — devices joined together to share and communicate — and that devices can connect with wires (wired) or without wires (wireless). Second, you learn to spot the many networks around us, and to name the devices on a home network and a school network. Third, you learn about the services on a network — the things you can do, like sharing files, sharing a printer, sending messages, and reaching the web. Fourth, they talk about the good things and the tricky things about networks (advantages and disadvantages). Fifth, they take a gentle first look at staying safe online.
outcomes: Say what a network is — devices joined together so they can share and communicate.
Know that devices connect with wires (wired) or without wires (wireless).
Name some devices found on a home network and a school network.
Describe services on a network — things you can do, such as sharing files, sharing a printer, communicating, and reaching the web.
Talk about one advantage (good thing) and one disadvantage (tricky thing) of a network.

concept-2-networks-around-us.explanation:
Networks are everywhere — in homes, schools, hospitals, shops and offices. The devices on a network depend on what the people need, so a home network and a school network do not have exactly the same devices.

In the classroom there are tablets and laptops. In the office there is a printer and a scanner — or one multifunction machine that does printing, scanning and copying all in one. On the wall there is an interactive smartboard, and a projector to show pictures big. All of these are joined on the school network.

concept-3-what-can-we-do-on-a-network-se.explanation:
The things we can do on a network are called services. The four main services are: sharing files (like photos and work), sharing a printer, communicating (sending messages and emails), and reaching the World Wide Web (the pages on the internet).

Maya saves her drawing on the network. Now Nora can open the very same drawing on a different tablet — that is sharing files. The whole class sends your work to one printer in the office — that is sharing a printer.
concept-3-what-can-we-do-on-a-network-se.example: The teacher sends a message to your parents — that is communicating. And when you look up facts about animals on a web page, you are using the World Wide Web.

concept-4-good-things-and-tricky-things-.explanation:
Networks have good things (we call these advantages) and tricky things (we call these disadvantages). Both are true at the same time — a network is very useful, and it also needs looking after.

Sharing is the big one. If the whole class shares one printer, that is cheaper than buying one for every tablet — so sharing saves money. You can share your work with a friend in a second.
concept-4-good-things-and-tricky-things-.example: You can work together even from different rooms. And your work is kept safely in one place, so it is easy to make a backup — an extra copy — in case anything is lost.

concept-5-staying-safe-online.explanation: Networks let us share and talk with people who are far away — that is wonderful. Staying safe online is a bit like crossing the road. Crossing the road is fine — we just look after ourselves, and a trusted grown-up helps us. Personal information — like your address, your phone number, or your school’s name — should stay private.
concept-5-staying-safe-online.example: Online is the same. We do not give private information to people or games we do not know.

comp-g03-u06.unitOverview: The unit builds three big skills. First, you learn to use logical thinking to plan a story with more than one character talking in order. Second, you learn to build programs that have more than one character, where some sprites have code and some are static objects (sprites that just sit there with no code, like a tree in the background). Third, you learn to make changes to your code to get the result you want — making a character talk for longer, changing the scene, or fixing a story whose steps are out of order.

comp-g03-u07.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 7 of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is all about the machines that computers control — and the most exciting of these is the robot. The big idea to hold onto the whole way through is simple: a computer or a robot only ever does what its instructions tell it to do. It does not think for itself. If we give it clear, correct steps in the right order, it does the job well. If our steps are wrong, it does the wrong thing — and it will not notice or fix it for us.

First, you learn that computers save our work as files, and that there are different types of file — text, audio (sound), image (picture), video, and games. Second, you learn that computers can control machines: a computer-controlled device takes an input and makes an output that tells the machine what to do. Third, you meet the Internet of Things — everyday objects like fridges and lightbulbs joined to the internet, called smart devices. Fourth, you learn what robots do, especially in factories: they move materials, build things, and check that work is good. The big skill on top is to give a robot a clear sequence of commands to guide it to a goal — and to spot and fix a command that is wrong.

concept-1-files-on-a-computer.explanation:
Computers save our work as files. There are different types of file — text, audio (sound), image (picture), video (moving pictures), and games. Every file has a name so we can find it again, and files are kept in folders, just like papers at home.

At home we keep important papers in folders so we can find them. A computer does the same. Everything we make on a computer is saved as a file, and each file has its own name.

concept-2-computers-control-machines.explanation:
Computers do more than save files — they can control machines. A computer-controlled device takes an input (something that goes in) and makes an output (something that comes out) which tells the machine what to do. The same machine can be made to do different jobs by changing its program.

When a car drives up, someone presses a button. That is the input. A little computer then lifts the barrier. That is the output.

concept-3-the-internet-of-things.example: A smart fridge is joined to the internet — it can notice the milk is finished and order more all by itself. Things joined to the internet like this are smart devices.

concept-4-robots-follow-commands-the-rob.explanation:
A robot is a computer-controlled device. It is given a program — a set of instructions — and it does exactly what the program says. In factories, robots have three main jobs: they handle materials (move boxes from place to place), they build things (join parts together), and they inspect (check that the work is good and safe). The most important idea of the whole unit lives here: a robot cannot think for itself. It only does what we tell it.

Try the Robot Game yourself: mark a start spot on the floor and place a goal a few steps away (a book for the library, or a cup for the well).

concept-5-give-the-robot-a-sequence-on-s.explanation:
We can give a robot a sequence of commands on the computer too. In Scratch we join blocks in the right order to move a robot to a goal. Just like the robot game, the order of the blocks matters.

Open Scratch at scratch.mit.edu and click Create. Click the little trash can on the cat to delete it, then click the Add Sprite button and choose the Robot sprite (any sprite is fine if you cannot find the robot).

comp-g03-u08.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 8 of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. You learn to make a computer play sounds and short tunes, and the big idea that sits under it: a program makes an output (like a sound) when it is given an input (like pressing a key). In this unit you become musicians — not with a real drum or flute, but with code. You already know this pattern from real life — press a doorbell and it rings; flick a switch and the light comes on.

There are four skills, taken straight from the textbook. Second, the headline skill, they predict the outcome of a change to an algorithm — if one step is different, what happens now? Third, they create a program that makes an output from an input — press a key or click a sprite, and a sound and a picture happen. Fourth, you learn the benefits of working with others when coding — sharing ideas, spotting mistakes, and being kind teammates.
outcomes: Predict the outcome of a simple sound algorithm by reading its steps in order.
Predict the outcome of a change to an algorithm — say what will be different when one step is changed.
Explain that a program makes an output (a sound, a picture) when it is given an input (a key press, a mouse click).
In Scratch, create a program that plays a sound and shows a picture when an input happens.
Understand that a tune is a sequence of notes in order, and that volume is how loud or quiet a sound is.
Change a program on purpose (a note, the volume, or a repeat) and check the outcome against a prediction.
Outline the benefits of working with others when creating programs.

concept-1-making-sounds-input-and-output.explanation: We can make lots of sounds with our bodies. Every sound has a start and then the sound itself. On a computer it is the same: something starts the program — the input — and then a sound comes out — the output. This input-then-output pattern is the heart of the whole unit. Try the four body sounds yourself: clap your hands, stomp your feet, snap your fingers, and slap your thigh. Then follow a short pattern, like: clap, clap, stomp, snap.

concept-2-reading-and-predicting-a-sound.explanation: An algorithm is a set of steps in the right order. If we read the steps carefully, we can predict the outcome — say what will happen before we run it. And if we change one step, we can predict what will be different. Predicting is the main skill of this unit. Here is one for when Leila claps her hands: read the sound algorithm below and act out each step as you go.

comp-g03-u09.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 9 of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is all about secret messages — how we can hide the meaning of a message so that only the right person can read it. The big idea is the cipher: a set of rules for turning a normal message into a secret one, and back again.

There are two important new words. Plain text is the normal, easy-to-read message, like hello. Ciphertext is the secret, scrambled version that only makes sense if you know the cipher. A cipher is the rule that turns one into the other, and both friends know the rule; anyone else just sees a jumble. We say we encode a message to make it secret, and decode it to read it again.
outcomes: Explain what a cipher is — a set of rules that turns plain text into ciphertext.

concept-1-what-is-a-cipher-plain-text-an.explanation: A cipher is a set of rules that turns a normal message into a secret one. The normal message is called plain text. The secret, scrambled message is called ciphertext. Both friends know the rule, so both can read it — but nobody else can. Have you ever wanted to tell your best friend something so that nobody else understands? Today we learn how to send secret messages — like a real spy or a code-breaker!

concept-2-the-flip-text-cipher.explanation: Our first real cipher is the flip-text cipher. The rule is simple: write the whole message backwards; to read it, flip it back. Same letters — just backwards. Now it is secret!

comp-g03-u10.unitOverview:
The first big idea is decomposition — a long word for a simple habit. When a job is too big to do all at once, we split it into smaller pieces called sub-tasks. Making a whole game is a big job, but “what the cat does when the game starts” is a small job, and “what the mouse does when you click it” is another. Each small job is easy to plan and to fix on its own.

The second big idea is that programmers learn from their mistakes. A mistake in a program is called an error or a bug, and bugs are completely normal — even the best programmers make them all day long. What matters is that we do not panic; we find the bug, fix it, and remember it. The third big idea, testing and debugging, is how we do that. To test means to run a program and check it does the right thing; to debug means to find the wrong part and fix it.

concept-1-breaking-a-big-task-into-sub-t.checkYourself: Can you name sensible sub-tasks — smaller than the whole job, but bigger than a single tiny step? Do not worry about perfect wording; the thinking is what matters.

concept-2-sub-tasks-in-a-game-events-sta.explanation:
In a Scratch game, each sub-task is started by an event — something that happens. The three events we use are: the green flag is clicked (the game starts), a sprite is clicked on, and a key is pressed. Each event runs its own little algorithm. So one sprite can have more than one sub-task, each with a different starting event.

Think about a light switch. Flicking it up turns the light on; flicking it down turns it off.

concept-3-mistakes-errors-and-being-a-bu.explanation:
Programs often have mistakes. A mistake in a program is called an error or a bug. Bugs are normal — every programmer makes them. We do not feel bad about a bug; we become a detective, find it, and fix it. Finding a bug even helps us, because we learn something and remember it next time.

A computer does exactly what your blocks say — not what you meant, but what you said. If a block is wrong, the computer still does it and you get a surprise.

comp-g03-u12.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 12, the very last unit of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. Be a Problem Solver. In this unit they pull their skills together around one big idea: every algorithm and every program has an input and an output. An input is the data we give to an algorithm — what we put in, or what starts it off. An output is the result — what comes out after the steps have run.

This unit names that idea and uses it to plan and build small programs. You already know inputs and outputs from everyday life, even without the words: press a button on the remote (input) and the channel changes (output); put fruit in a blender (input) and out comes a smoothie (output).
outcomes: Identify the input(s) and the output of an algorithm, in everyday activities and in written steps.
Understand that an input is the data we give to an algorithm, and an output is the result of processing it.
Create a simple algorithm that turns an input into an output, such as a number machine.
Break a big job into small steps in the right order (decomposition).
In Scratch, use an event block (green flag, sprite clicked, key pressed) as the input that starts a program.
In Scratch, build a program that resets a sprite to its starting costume and position.
Plan, test and fix a program — find a bug, correct it, and run it again.

concept-1-inputs-and-outputs-are-everywh.explanation:
Every algorithm has an input and an output. The input is the data we give it — what we put in, or the thing that starts it. The output is the result we get out. Inputs and outputs are all around us, every single day.

Watch. I press this button — that is the input, the thing I put in.
concept-1-inputs-and-outputs-are-everywh.example: The television changes channel — that is the output, the result. Input goes in, output comes out.
concept-1-inputs-and-outputs-are-everywh.checkYourself: A common slip is to name the machine (the blender) as the input — gently steer you to the thing we put in (the fruit) and the result that comes out (the smoothie). Can you point to the input (what goes in / what starts it) and the output (the result)?

concept-2-break-a-big-job-into-small-ste.checkYourself: Can you point to which steps are the inputs and which is the output? Can you list the steps in a sensible order? Do not worry about perfect wording — the thinking is what matters.

concept-4-code-the-reset-in-scratch.explanation: Now we turn our plan into a real program. In Scratch we join coloured blocks. The block at the very top that starts everything is called an event block (it is shaped like a hat). The event block is our input. The blocks under it are the outputs — the actions that happen. Delete the cat sprite, add the Horse sprite (the Add Sprite button, bottom right), and choose the Farm backdrop. Open Scratch at scratch.mit.edu and click Create.

concept-5-test-it-and-fix-the-bugs.explanation:
A real problem solver does not stop when the program is built. You test it — run it and watch carefully — and if it does not do what the plan said, they hunt for the bug and fix it. Finding and fixing a bug is called debugging, and it is the most important problem-solving skill of all.

Even the best coders get bugs. A bug is not a failure — it is a clue.

comp-g04-u01.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 1 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. You learn how a computer can make a character move by repeating instructions, and use that idea to build simple animations in Scratch. The big new idea is repetition — doing something over and over — and the tool for repetition in Scratch is the Forever block.

An animation is just a set of pictures shown one after another, fast, so it looks like movement. When you make a butterfly flap its wings forever, they are watching a loop happen before their eyes.

First, to follow, understand and correct algorithms that use repetition — to read steps, spot where they repeat, and fix them if they are wrong. Second, to add comments to your code — short notes that explain what it does, like a label on a jar. Third, to develop programs with repetition in Scratch using the Forever block, so a character repeats an action without stopping.
outcomes: Follow, understand and correct algorithms that use repetition — read steps that repeat, say what job they do, and fix them when a step is wrong.
Understand what a forever loop is — instructions that repeat over and over without stopping.
Add comments to blocks of code to explain what the code does.
Develop programs with repetition in Scratch using the Forever block.
Build a simple animation by switching costumes and moving a sprite inside a forever loop.

concept-1-what-is-repetition-loops-all-a.explanation:
Repetition means doing something over and over. Loops are all around us — many things in the world repeat again and again. In computing, we use repetition to make a character repeat an action, and that is how animation works.

How did you know what to do next? Doing something over and over is called repetition. Start with a clapping game.

concept-4-adding-comments-and-a-walking-.explanation:
A comment is a note we add to our code to explain what it does. Comments help other people (and our future selves) understand the program, and help with debugging — finding and fixing mistakes. Unlike the rest of the code, a comment does not run. We will also make a chick that walks and changes costume forever.

The label does not change what is inside — it just reminds us. A comment is like a label for our code. Right-click a block. Choose Add Comment.

concept-5-animating-a-moving-character-a.explanation:
We put together everything we know — repetition, the Forever block, moving, switching costumes, and comments — to animate a character that moves side to side, and we add a sound.

Add the Ballerina sprite (a built-in Scratch character) and the Theater 2 backdrop. We want the character to sway right, then back left, over and over.

concept-3-your-first-animation-in-scratc.explanation:
In Scratch we join coloured blocks to make a program. To repeat blocks over and over, we drop them inside the Forever block, in the Control group. Everything inside it repeats until we stop the program. We will use it to make a butterfly flap forever.

Open scratch.mit.edu and click Create. Delete the cat, click Add Sprite and choose Butterfly 2, then choose the Blue Sky backdrop.

concept-2-forever-loops-in-algorithms-un.explanation:
A forever loop is repetition where the instructions repeat over and over without stopping. Instead of writing the same step again and again, we write it once and say “repeat forever”. March on the spot, forever. That is a forever loop.

Try it: Follow the steps out loud first, then fill the gaps.

Check yourself: Can you replace a repeated step with “repeat forever” instead of copying it many times? Do you understand that a forever loop repeats until you stop it?
