comp-g04-u02.unitOverview: The unit teaches four connected ideas. First, what a database is, and the difference between a physical and a digital database. Second, that every database is built from records and fields — each record is all the data about one thing (one row), and each field is one piece of data (one column, with a heading). Fourth, how to collect data with a form, how to search a database to find records, and how to sort data into ascending and descending order.
outcomes: Say what a database is (an organised collection of related data) and give examples.
Tell the difference between a physical (paper) and a digital (computer) database, and give one advantage of each.
Name the parts of a database: a record (one row — all the data about one thing) and a field (one column, with a heading).
Explain the difference between data (raw facts) and information (processed data that has meaning).
Give some advantages and disadvantages of using a form to collect data.
Search a small database to find the records that match.
Sort data into ascending (A-Z, small to large) and descending (Z-A, large to small) order, by hand and in a spreadsheet.

concept-1-what-is-a-database-physical-an.explanation:
A database is an organised collection of related data. A phone's contact list is a database. A database can be physical (kept on paper) or digital (kept on a computer). Every database is made of records and fields: each record is all the data about one thing (one row), and each field is one piece of data (one column, with a heading).

Imagine the teacher at Ehel Academy writes each pupil's details on a sheet of paper and keeps every sheet in a filing cabinet. That is a physical database — it is on paper. It works, but searching for one pupil takes time, changing a sheet is messy, and it needs a lot of space. Now imagine the same details are typed into the computer.

concept-2-data-and-information.explanation:
Information is what we get after the data has been processed, sorted and given meaning. Data answers “what are the facts?” ; information answers “so what do the facts tell us?”

What do these numbers mean? Now add the missing meaning: “These are the numbers of books six pupils in the reading club read this term.” Suddenly we can work things out: Maya read the most (20 books), Sana read the fewest (7), and the club read 74 books in total. Those useful facts are information — the data has been processed.

concept-5-sort-a-database-on-the-compute.explanation:

Type the headings in the first row and the six records underneath. Watch — by hand this took us a few minutes. The computer will do it in one second.

comp-g04-u03.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 3 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is all about networks. A network is a group of computers and devices joined together so they can share — share files, share a printer, and send each other messages. You already live inside networks every day: the computers at Ehel Academy that reach the same printer, the Wi-Fi the family's phones join at home, and the internet that carries a message from Hargeisa to Mogadishu are all networks at work.

First, a network has two kinds of computer: a server, which gives out services (it stores, finds and sends files, and lets computers share and talk), and a client, which asks the server for what it needs. You meet the file, web, print and mail servers, and see a client send a request and the server send back a response. Second, the difference between the internet (all the world's networks joined together) and the World Wide Web (one service on it: the web pages we open in a browser). Third, that networks can be wired (ethernet cables) or wireless (Wi-Fi, using radio waves), and when each is better.
outcomes: Explain that a network is computers joined together to share files, devices and messages.
Say what a server does and what a client does, and give an example of each.
Name different servers (file, web, print, mail) and match each to its job.
Describe how a client sends a request and a server sends back a response.
Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
Say what a browser, a hyperlink and a website are.
Describe the difference between a wired (ethernet) and a wireless (Wi-Fi) network.
Choose wired or wireless for a situation and give a reason — being a network designer.
Follow simple rules to help keep a network, and themselves, safe online.

concept-1-what-is-a-network-servers-and-.explanation:
A network is computers and devices joined together so they can share — files, a printer, messages. It has two kinds of computer. A server gives out services: it stores, finds and sends files, and lets the other computers share things and talk to one another. A client is a computer that asks the server for what it needs, like a file or a web page.

One child is the waiter; the others are customers. Each customer asks for something; the waiter finds it and brings it back. Afterwards ask: what was the waiter's job? (To serve.) The customer's? (To ask.) Then reveal the secret: “On a network the waiter is the server and the customers are the clients — the customer asks, and the server serves.”

concept-2-meet-the-servers-and-how-a-req.explanation:
A network can have more than one server, each with its own job. A file server stores files for everyone. A web server holds and sends web pages. A print server sends documents to a printer. A mail server passes emails between people. (Others exist too, like an application server for running programs, but these four are the main ones.) Whatever the server, the pattern is the same: the client sends a request, and the server sends back a response.

A big restaurant might have one waiter just for drinks, one just for meals, and one just for desserts — each does its own job. A network is the same: different servers for different jobs.

concept-3-the-internet-and-the-world-wid.explanation:
The internet is a worldwide network of networks — all the world's networks joined together, linking millions of computers, phones and tablets. The World Wide Web is not the same: the Web is just one service on the internet — a huge collection of web pages we open with a browser. Email, video calls and messaging also run on the internet, but are not the Web. A hyperlink jumps you from one web page to another; a group of linked pages is a website.

This is the trickiest idea of the unit, so use a picture. The internet is like a huge country with roads joining every town.
concept-3-the-internet-and-the-world-wid.example: The World Wide Web is like all the libraries in that country — wonderful to visit, but only one of the things the roads reach. Email vans and video-call vans use the same roads, but they are not libraries.
concept-3-the-internet-and-the-world-wid.checkYourself: Can you give an example of something on the internet that is not the Web (email, a video call)? Do not worry if this takes time — even adults mix these up.

concept-4-wired-and-wireless-ethernet-an.explanation:
A network can be wired or wireless. A wired network joins its devices with cables — the cables are called ethernet. A wireless network joins its devices through the air using invisible radio waves, and the set of rules the devices use to do this is called Wi-Fi. Each kind is better for different jobs.

A wired network is like being joined by a rope — strong, fast and steady, but you cannot walk away. A wireless network is like calling across a room — free to move, but weaker the further you go, and others might overhear. Wired is faster and more secure; wireless lets you move.

concept-5-be-a-network-designer-and-keep.explanation:
A good designer asks: what do we want to share? which computer is the server? which are the clients? and should each device be wired or wireless? At the same time, we keep the network — and ourselves — safe, because a network (especially wireless) can be reached by outsiders if we are not careful.

Nadia learnt about networks at Ehel Academy, and wants to help her family join their computer, phones and tablets into one network to share photos and reach the printer. But her family ask: what is a network? who is the server? cables or Wi-Fi?

comp-g04-u04.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 4 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. Be a Storyteller. It is a unit about repetition — the way stories and songs, and computer programs, do the same thing again and again. You become storytellers who notice that a good story is full of repeats, and then you learn how a computer handles a repeat neatly using a loop.

Think of how many stories work: a character knocks three times, three travellers ask the same question, a song's chorus comes back after every verse. In our own day we repeat actions too, like stirring a pot round and round. Repetition is everywhere — and that is the big idea of this unit. In computing we give it a name: iteration.

First, a loop is a set of instructions that is repeated. Second, one single pass through those instructions is called an iteration — so if a loop runs four times, there are four iterations. Third, a counter keeps track of how many times the loop has run, and a loop that repeats a set, known number of times is called a count-controlled loop. Fourth, you learn to use repetition to make a long algorithm shorter, and then to build it in Scratch with the Repeat block.
outcomes: Explain that a loop is a set of instructions that is repeated, and give an example from a story or a song.
Understand that an iteration is one single pass through the repeated steps, and count the iterations in an algorithm.
Understand that a counter keeps track of how many times a loop has run.
Recognise a count-controlled loop — a loop that repeats a set (known) number of times.
Use repetition to make a long algorithm shorter, keeping the same result.
Follow and correct an algorithm that uses repetition (put a jumbled story back in order).
In Scratch, build a program using the Repeat block (a count-controlled loop) and change the counter number.

concept-1-stories-that-repeat-loops-and-.explanation:
A loop is a set of instructions that is repeated. When we go through those instructions one time, that is one iteration. If the loop runs several times, there are several iterations.

Start with a story — storytellers already know all about repeats. Tell it slowly, counting the repeats on your fingers.

concept-3-into-scratch-the-repeat-block.explanation:
The same idea works on the computer. In Scratch, the Repeat block is a count-controlled loop. It is a C-shaped block from the Control group: you drop the steps you want to repeat inside its mouth, and you type the counter number at the top.

First build the LONG way — the repeated blocks written out four times — and run it with the green flag. Open Scratch at scratch.mit.edu, click Create, and keep the Cat sprite (it has two costumes, so it looks like it is walking). Choose a simple backdrop like Blue Sky. Our storyteller cat is going to walk across to greet a friend, taking four steps.

concept-5-tell-your-repeating-story-put-.explanation:
You build a short Scratch story where a count-controlled loop does the repeating part. Changing the counter number changes how many times the repeat happens — so the storyteller is in control.

Long ago, on a clear night, Nora looked up and counted the stars. Add the Star sprite and a night backdrop (like Stars or Night City), make sure the Pen extension is on (for the stamp block), and build this together

comp-g04-u05.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 5 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit answers two big questions: What does a computer scientist actually do? and How do robots help people at work? Now you meet the real people who do this for a living, and discover that the clever machines around us — from a delivery drone to a robot that helps a doctor — were built by computer scientists.
outcomes: Say what a computer scientist is — a person who uses computational thinking to work with computer hardware and software.
Name some roles a computer scientist can have (hardware engineer, games developer/programmer, software developer, data analyst, robotics engineer).
Describe what almost all computer scientists do: look at a problem and decide how to solve it, break a big problem into smaller ones, and work in a team.
Give examples of robots in delivery, transport, food and healthcare, and say what each does.
Explain what a sensor is and what a drone is.
Think like a computer scientist by writing a simple algorithm (steps in the right order) for a robot to follow.

concept-1-what-is-a-computer-scientist.explanation:
A computer scientist is a person who uses computational thinking — solving a problem by breaking it into clear steps — to work with computer hardware and software. They create, design and build things to solve problems: writing the software for an app, helping design a robot to pack boxes in a factory, or building a new computer part.

On your way here you passed traffic lights, a car, a phone, the fridge at home. Every one has a computer inside, and a computer scientist helped make it work. A computer scientist is someone who is very good at solving problems with computers — by thinking in steps.

concept-2-so-many-roles-meet-five-comput.explanation: A computer scientist can have many different roles — you will meet five. Yet in almost every role they do the same three things: look at a problem and decide how to solve it, break a big problem into smaller ones, and work as part of a team — often with people who know little about computing, like artists and shopkeepers.

concept-3-robots-at-work-delivery-and-tr.explanation:
Robots are machines that can be programmed to do tasks, and they help people in many industries. Today, two: delivery and transport. For delivery, some companies use flying robots called drones to carry packages, and some restaurants use small ground robots to bring food. For transport, a driverless vehicle (also called an AV) drives itself using sensors — devices that detect things around it, like other cars and the road edge. There are driverless cars, buses and even trains.

When a package arrives, a person usually brings it. But some companies now use a drone — a little flying machine with no pilot on board, controlled from far away — to fly it to you. Others use a small robot on wheels on the pavement. A driverless car has no human driver.
concept-3-robots-at-work-delivery-and-tr.example: So how does it not crash? It is covered in sensors — devices that sense what is around the car, like eyes and ears made of electronics — and its computer uses them to steer safely.

concept-4-robots-at-work-food-and-health.explanation:
Two more industries. In the food service industry, robot waiters can greet customers, take an order, serve food and clear dishes, and some robots even prepare food. In healthcare, robots can help surgeons during operations, robotic limbs (a robotic arm or hand) help injured or disabled people pick up and hold objects, and care robots can check a patient's temperature, bring medicine, and help keep hospitals clean.

Imagine a cafe where a friendly robot rolls up, greets you and brings your food — that is a robot in the food service industry. In a hospital, a robot can help a doctor operate very steadily.

concept-5-think-like-a-computer-scientis.explanation: A robot only knows what to do because someone wrote it an algorithm — a set of steps in the right order. Choose a job everyone can picture: a delivery robot taking a package from the shop to a house. Write the steps in order, from picking up the package to putting it down at the house.

comp-g04-u06.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 6 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. Be a Musician. But do not be fooled by the musical title: the real computing idea in this unit is repetition — teaching the computer to do something again and again. Music is simply the fun, natural way to meet that idea, because music is full of repeating beats and repeating choruses.

The computing word for repetition is iteration — repeating the same block of code over and over. Learning when to use each loop is the heart of the unit. You meet three ways to repeat in Scratch: the forever loop, which never stops; the repeat ( ) loop, which repeats a set number of times and then stops; and the repeat until ( ) loop, which keeps going until something becomes true, such as a key being pressed.

They predict the outcome of an algorithm before running it — reading the steps to work out what they will hear. And they compare and contrast two algorithms written for the same task, deciding which is better suited (if you want a beat exactly three times and then stop, is forever or repeat (3) the right tool?).

comp-g04-u07.unitOverview: The big idea is the data table — a grid with rows and columns. You then learn about data types — the kind of data a field is allowed to hold — and finally how to search a data table to answer real questions, such as “How many items are in the Snacks section?” In Sessions 4 and 5 you move the same skills onto a computer, building a small data table in a free spreadsheet. Most of this unit is unplugged: you draw and label data tables in your notebook, sort facts by type, and search tables by hand. Alongside the content, you practise two thinking skills from the syllabus: you group items that belong together, and you decide which field to look in before you start a search.

concept-1-data-data-tables-records-and-f.explanation: A database is an organised collection of facts. We keep data organised so we can find it quickly. The tidiest way is a data table — a grid of rows and columns.
concept-1-data-data-tables-records-and-f.example: A field is a column (one kind of information, like Age); a record is a row (everything about one child); and a data item is one fact in one cell (like the 9 in Leila’s Age cell). Data (raw facts: “Leila”, “9”) is different from information (“Leila is 9 years old”).

concept-2-data-types-unplugged.explanation: Every field has a data type — the kind of data it is allowed to hold. Teach the four main types: Text (letters and other characters), Number (only numbers, and you can do sums with them), Date/Time (a date or a time), and Yes/No (only one of two values).
concept-2-data-types-unplugged.example: Then add Currency as the money type — a Number shown with a money sign like $3.00. The key rule: every cell in one field must use the same data type and format.

concept-3-searching-a-data-table-to-answ.explanation: People keep data so they can answer questions with it. To search a data table, use two steps: Step 1 — choose the right field (which column has the answer?), then Step 2 — scan, count or match down that field. This “field first” habit is the thinking skill of the unit: decide where to look before you look.

concept-4-from-paper-to-screen-a-data-ta.explanation:
The same data table works on a computer, where it is quicker to change and search. A spreadsheet is a giant grid: columns have letters (A, B, C...), rows have numbers (1, 2, 3...), and each box is a cell with an address like A1. The header row (row 1) holds the field names; each record goes on its own row underneath.

This is exactly the layout you will build. Follow each step in order and copy it carefully.

comp-g04-u08.unitOverview:
Behind the fun theme sit three solid computing ideas. The first is inputs and outputs. An input is data that goes into a computer (a key press, a click, a sound at the microphone), and the hardware that sends it in is an input device. An output is information the computer sends back out to us (a picture on the screen, a sound from the speaker), and the hardware that carries it out is an output device. The headline objective of the whole unit is to build a program that produces different outputs from different inputs — press one key and something happy happens, press another and something different happens.

The second idea is decomposition — breaking a big problem into smaller parts. When our badge has to do two different things, decomposition tells us we actually need two separate algorithms, one for each job. The third idea is writing and reading algorithms: setting out the steps in order (we use a simple table), predicting what an algorithm will do before we run it, and picking out its components (what starts it, what it shows, how long for, and how many times it repeats).

concept-1-inputs-and-outputs-all-around-.explanation:
A computer takes in inputs and gives back outputs. An input is data going in; an output is information coming out. The hardware that carries data in is an input device (keyboard, mouse, microphone, touchscreen, camera); the hardware that carries information out is an output device (screen, speaker, headphones, printer).

You have five amazing input devices of your own — your senses. Your eyes take in sight, your ears take in sound, your nose takes in smell, your tongue takes in taste, your skin takes in touch.

comp-g04-u09.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 9 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is called “Be a Code Cracker”, and it is all about keeping information safe. It is one of the most exciting units of the year, and — happily — it needs no computers at all. Everything is done with a pencil, paper and a bit of clever thinking.

There are three big ideas, and they fit together like a story. First, why do we need secrets? Because so much information now travels over networks and the internet — and when a network breaks (a network failure), or a bad person tries to steal information, that information is in danger. Second, the way we protect it is encryption: we disguise a message so only a person with the secret key can understand it.

The word cipher simply means a secret way of writing: to encrypt is to turn a normal message (plain text) into a scrambled one (ciphertext), and to decrypt is to turn it back. These are not made-up school codes — the Caesar cipher is over two thousand years old, used by the Roman leader Julius Caesar, and the Pigpen cipher has been used since the 1500s.
outcomes: Explain that a network failure is when a fault in hardware or software stops a network working properly.
Give examples of problems caused by a network failure in a hospital, a school, for the police, and in a shop or bank.
Explain that encryption disguises a message so that only someone with the secret key can understand it.
Use the words plain text (before) and ciphertext (after), and say where and why encryption is used.
Explain that a cipher is a secret way of writing, and that Caesar and Pigpen are substitution ciphers (one letter is swapped for something else).
Encrypt and decrypt a message using the Caesar cipher with a chosen key, and know what to do when a letter goes past Z (wrap around to A).
Encrypt and decrypt a message using the Pigpen cipher, reading the symbols from the grid.
Invent a simple cipher of their own and understand why the person receiving a message needs the key.

concept-1-networks-and-what-happens-when.explanation:
A network is a set of computers and devices joined together so they can share things — files, messages and the internet. A network failure is when a fault in the hardware (the machines or cables) or the software (the programs) stops the network working properly. When the network is down, people cannot share files, send emails, reach the internet, or get to the information stored on the network.

Start with a hook that shows why secrets matter.

concept-2-what-is-encryption-and-why-do-.explanation: Encryption means disguising a message so that only certain people can understand it. It uses a key — the secret that explains how the message has been disguised. The normal message is called plain text; the disguised message is called ciphertext. A very important idea: encryption does not stop someone seeing the letters of a message — it stops them understanding it. Even if someone snatches it, they just see “KHOOR” and cannot understand it. Only the person with the same key can decrypt it back to “HELLO”.

concept-4-cracking-the-caesar-cipher-dec.explanation:
To decrypt a Caesar message you do the opposite of encrypting: shift each letter the same number of places backwards. If the key was 3, move each letter 3 places back. On the alphabet strip, find the letter on the bottom row and read off the normal letter above it.

With a key of 3, decrypt KHOOR back to HELLO (K to H, H to E, O to L, O to L, R to O). Then try a whole sentence from the textbook, corrected here so it is exactly right: decrypt VHH BRX WRQLJKW with a key of 3 to reveal SEE YOU TONIGHT. Cracking a real sentence together is a thrilling moment — you can shout out the words as they appear.

concept-3-the-caesar-cipher-writing-secr.explanation:
The Caesar cipher is one of the oldest ways to encrypt. You shift every letter along the alphabet by the same number of places. That number is the key. Julius Caesar himself often used a key of 3. Because you swap each letter for another letter, it is called a substitution cipher.

The top row is the normal alphabet; the bottom row is the same alphabet shifted along by 3. To encrypt, find your letter on the top and write the letter underneath it, using the Caesar alphabet strip below.

comp-g04-u10.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 10 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. But here is the important part for you. This is not a unit about high scores or timers; it is about two big ideas that make games work: sub-routines and repetition. The game is the joyful reason to learn them.

The first big idea is the sub-routine: a set of instructions for a job you do again and again, written once and then run whenever you need it. Getting ready for school is a sub-routine — pack your bag, put on your shoes, check you have your lunch — and you do not re-learn those steps every morning; you just do the routine again. In our game, every time the player moves the cat the same little job happens (change costume, a small meow), so instead of writing it four times, once per arrow key, we write it once as Move Around.

The second big idea is repetition. A forever loop repeats without ever stopping (this is repetition), while a repeat (6) loop repeats a set number of times and then stops (this is iteration, the count-controlled loop from Unit 4). In our game, a repeat loop makes the treat spin before the chase begins.
outcomes: Explain that a sub-routine is a set of instructions for a frequently-used job, made once and run many times.
In Scratch, make a sub-routine with My Blocks (Make a Block) and run it from other scripts.
Explain the difference between a forever loop (repetition — never stops) and a repeat (n) loop (iteration — a set number of times).
Recognise the event blocks that start a script: when green flag clicked, when key pressed, and when this sprite clicked.
Use coordinates to move a sprite: change x by, change y by, and glide or go to a random position.
Build a small, working game in Scratch that uses a sub-routine and a loop.
Test a program systematically — checking each part in turn — to find an error, and debug (fix) it.

comp-g04-u11.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 11 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is all about control systems — and the friendly way we meet them is through robots. The big idea is simple and powerful: a control system, and a robot, always works in three steps. It takes in input (it senses the world), it processes that information (its brain decides what to do), and it makes an output (it acts). We say a robot can sense, think and act.

You meet sensors — special input devices that detect changes in the world, such as distance, light, motion, temperature and infrared sensors. You meet the data logger, a device left alone to sense and store data over time. You learn about output devices — screens, printers, lights, sounds and movement (a robot's motors and arm). And you learn the difference between application software (programs that do a job for you) and system software (like the operating system, that runs the machine itself), and that different files need different amounts of storage.
outcomes: Explain that a control system works in three steps: input (sense), process (decide), output (act) — and that a robot is a control system.
Give examples of everyday control systems (rice cooker, streetlight, traffic lights, fridge) and point to their input, process and output.
Say what a sensor is, and name sensors that detect distance, light, motion, temperature and infrared.
Explain what a data logger is and how it is used.
Name output devices — screen, printer, light, sound (buzzer/speaker), and movement (motor, robotic arm).
Tell the difference between application software and system software, and say what an operating system is.
Order everyday files from the smallest to the biggest storage (text, audio, image, video).
Follow (trace) a set of commands to guide a robot on a grid, and fix a command list that has a mistake.

concept-1-sense-think-act-what-a-control.explanation: A control system is a machine that works in three steps. It takes input (it senses the world), it processes the input (its brain, the processor, decides what to do), and it makes an output (it acts — it moves, lights up, or makes a sound). A robot is a control system that we build to do a job for us. The short way to remember it is sense — think — act. Try acting it out yourself: notice something around you (“a wall in front!”) — that is input. Decide a rule (“if there is a wall, stop and turn”) — that is process.
concept-1-sense-think-act-what-a-control.example: Then do the turn — that is output. You just acted as a robot — you sensed, you thought, and you acted.

concept-2-sensing-the-world-sensors-and-.explanation:
The input usually comes from a sensor — a special input device that detects a change in the world and sends that information to the processor. Different sensors sense different things: distance (how close something is), light (bright or dark), motion (movement), temperature (heat and cold), and infrared (the invisible signal from a remote). A data logger contains a sensor, a processor and storage, and is left alone to gather data over time.

Light sensor: cup your hands over a torch — “A streetlight senses the dark and switches itself on.” Temperature sensor: the rice cooker from the source senses the heat of the rice and turns down when it is cooked. Distance sensor: hold a hand near a wall — “A robot senses when a wall is close and stops before it bumps.” Infrared sensor: point a TV remote and press a button — “The remote sends an invisible signal the TV senses.” Motion sensor: walk towards an imaginary door — “It senses you move, and the light comes on.”

concept-3-acting-on-the-world-outputs-an.explanation:
The output takes what the processor decided and makes something happen we can see, hear or feel. Output devices include a screen (text, pictures, video), a printer, lights (a bulb or lamp), sound (a buzzer, speaker or bell) and movement (a motor turning wheels, or a robotic arm that lifts things). A robot's wheels and arm are outputs. When the processor decides to move, it sends commands to the motors — so guiding a robot across the floor is really the output stage in action.

Sort outputs by the sense they use. “Which do we see?” — a screen, a printed page, a lamp. “Which do we hear?” — a buzzer, a speaker, a bell.
concept-3-acting-on-the-world-outputs-an.example: “Which move?” — a motor spinning a wheel, a robotic arm on a date farm lifting a box. Link each output back to a sensor: a smoke alarm senses smoke (input) and sounds a buzzer (output); a robot senses a wall (input) and its motors stop (output).

concept-4-the-software-that-runs-a-robot.explanation:
A robot or computer needs software — the programs that tell it what to do — and there are two kinds. Application software does a job for the user: a word processor, a spreadsheet, a browser, a music player, a game — and a robot's own task program. System software runs the machine itself: it manages files and memory, keeps the machine safe, decides which task runs first, and controls the input and output devices. The most important piece is the operating system, which oversees everything quietly in the background.

Application software is like a cook who makes one dish — the writing dish, the game dish. System software is the kitchen manager, the operating system, who keeps the kitchen running and makes sure the taps and cookers work. You notice the cook's dish; you rarely notice the manager — but nothing works without them. the operating system. a web browser. virus protection. a music app. the program that manages the files.

concept-5-a-robot-s-memory-file-sizes-an.explanation:
A robot or computer stores its work as files, and different files need different amounts of storage. From smallest to biggest: a text file (a note) is tiny; an audio file (a song) is bigger; an image file (a photo) bigger still; a video file (a film) is the biggest of all. Games vary, depending on how many pictures, sounds and videos they hold. Then we bring the unit together: a robot senses (input), thinks (process), acts (output), runs on software, and stores files.

Imagine packing each file into a suitcase. A text note is one folded shirt — it barely fills the case. A song needs a bigger case.

comp-g04-u12.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 12 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy — the very last unit of the year. Be an Artist. But there is no paper and no paintbrush: the canvas is a tiny computer called the micro:bit, and the paint is light. The micro:bit has 25 little red lights — LEDs — in a 5-by-5 grid. By turning those lights on and off, we can draw a square, a heart, a diamond, an arrow, or our own repeating pattern, like the geometric tile-work in a mosaic.

the artistic title hides a serious computing idea: physical computing. A micro:bit is a physical computing device — a small computer that senses the world and acts on it. It takes in inputs (a button press, a touch, a shake) and gives out outputs (a shape of light, a sound). The big idea is that we can program different outputs from different inputs: Button A shows a square, Button B shows a heart, touching the gold logo plays a twinkle sound.

The repeat ( ) loop repeats a set number of times and then stops (a count-controlled loop, met earlier this year); the forever loop repeats over and over and never stops. A flashing dot, a twinkling pattern, a blinking arrow — all are loops at work. You also make their art move, using two kinds of loop — blocks that repeat other blocks. And as always, you write the algorithm first (a simple plan) and only then build the code, because a good artist and a good programmer both plan before they start.
outcomes: Explain that a micro:bit is a physical computing device — a small computer that senses the world and acts on it.
Tell the difference between an input (information going into the device, like a button press) and an output (information coming out, like a shape of light or a sound).
Name some inputs on the micro:bit (Button A, Button B, the touch logo, shake) and some outputs (the LED display, the speaker).
Draw a shape or pattern on the 5-by-5 LED grid using the show leds, show icon and show arrow blocks in MakeCode.
Develop an algorithm (a plan) so that different inputs produce different outputs, then build it as a program.
Build a program with a count-controlled loop (the repeat ( ) block) to flash art a set number of times.
Build a program with a forever loop to make art animate over and over.
Test a program part by part, and find and fix (debug) simple mistakes.

steps: Open makecode.microbit.org for blocks, or python.microbit.org for Python.
Write your code in the editor.
The micro:bit simulator on the left runs your code straight away.
Click the on-screen A and B buttons, and use the shake control, to test your inputs.

comp-g05-u01.unitOverview:
Hello, and welcome to Unit 1 of Year 5 Computing at Ehel Academy! This is the biggest and most exciting unit of the year. In it, you will learn to think like a real computer programmer and to build working programs that solve real problems. A computer only ever does exactly what you tell it, so the skill you are growing is the skill of giving clear, correct instructions. We call this way of thinking computational thinking.

This unit has seven parts, which we call subunits. Each one gives you a new tool for your programming toolbox. You will learn to store information in variables, do maths and comparisons with operators, let your program make decisions with selection, plan a solution before you build it, make objects interact in a game, build programs that are user-friendly, and finally put a program onto a tiny hand-held computer called the micro:bit.

1.6 Creating user-friendly programs — learn the roles and stages of making software, and judge a program against clear criteria.

steps: Open makecode.microbit.org for blocks, or python.microbit.org for Python.
Write your code in the editor.
The micro:bit simulator on the left runs your code straight away.
Click the on-screen A and B buttons, and use the shake control, to test your inputs.

concept-1-assigning-variables.explanation:
A variable is a named box that stores a piece of data. The special thing about a variable is that the value inside it can change while the program runs. You can put a value in, use it later, and change it whenever you need to. A variable can only hold one value at a time: if you put a new value in, the old one is gone, just like a box that can hold only one thing.

The data we store is called a value. A value can be a number (like 10), some text (like Leila), or a symbol. When we put a value into a variable, we say we assign the value to the variable.

You have used variables before without knowing it. Think about a count-controlled loop — a loop that repeats an exact number of times. The number of repeats is stored in a variable, often called Count:

A count-controlled loop; the variable Count stores the number of repeats

Here Count is a variable. Its value is 4, so the loop repeats 4 times. If you change the value to set Count to 2, the very same loop now repeats only 2 times. You did not rewrite the loop — you just changed the value inside the variable. That is the power of a variable.

A variable name should be meaningful — it should tell you what is stored inside. The name Count tells you it stores how many times to repeat. A name like x tells you nothing. Good names make your program much easier to read, both for you and for anyone else who uses it.

The word 'algorithm' comes from the name of a great scholar who lived over 1,000 years ago: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi. The word 'algebra' also comes from the title of one of his books. Every time you say 'algorithm', you are remembering a brilliant mathematician!

Imagine a program that makes a birthday card. The card says 'Happy Birthday', then the person's name and age. The name and age change depending on whose birthday it is, so we store them in variables. For Sami's card we assign the values like this:

Assigning a text value and a number value

Now the program can use these variables to build the message. The variable Name holds the text Sami, and the variable Age holds the number 10. If it were Nadia's birthday and she is turning 8, we would simply assign set Name to Nadia and set Age to 8, and the same program would make her card. We change the values, not the program.

Displaying what is inside a variable

Let us follow another example. Sami stores his favourite fruit in a well-named variable, then displays it:

Trace the result. The variable MyFavouriteFruit is assigned the value banana. The say instruction then outputs what is inside the variable, so the program says banana. If Leila used the same program, she might write set MyFavouriteFruit to mango, and it would say mango. The variable holds a temporary value — temporary means it is not kept forever and can be changed for a different user.

Variables in Scratch: Leila's basketball scoreboard

Now let us build a real program in Scratch. Leila wants a basketball scoreboard. In basketball, a basket scored from inside the three-point line is worth 2 points, and one scored from outside it is worth 3 points. First, in Scratch, click Variables in the blocks palette, then Make a Variable, name it Score, and choose For all sprites. Do the same to make a variable called Shots.

Here is the code. Each basketball is a sprite. When you click a basketball, it means someone scored, so the score and the shot counter both change:

concept-2-using-operators.explanation:
An operator is a symbol that does an action on values. In this subunit you meet two families of operators: arithmetic operators for doing maths, and comparison operators for comparing values.

Arithmetic is the use of numbers in calculations, such as adding or subtracting. The two most important arithmetic operators are + for addition and - for subtraction. (Computers can also multiply with * and divide with /, but in this unit we focus on + and -.) For example, 7 + 6 tells the computer to add 7 and 6, and 10 - 3 tells it to subtract 3 from 10.

We can use arithmetic operators with variables, not just plain numbers. Here is the classic example:

Adding two variables and storing the answer in a third variable

Trace the result. First, 7 is assigned to FirstNumber and 6 is assigned to SecondNumber. Then the computer adds the values inside those two variables: 7 + 6 = 13. The answer 13 is assigned to the variable Result. So the value of Result is 13. Because we used variables, we can change the two numbers without rewriting the calculation.

Remember two rules that catch people out. First, a variable holds only the last value assigned to it: if you set Balls to 1, then set Balls to 2, then set Balls to 3, the value of Balls is 3. Second, instructions run in sequence, one after another, from top to bottom.

Sometimes we do not know a value until the program runs. Think of Sami's little sister Nadia using a calculator: the numbers change every time. This is where user input comes in — the user provides the data. In Scratch, the ask [ ] and wait block (in the Sensing section) lets the user type on the keyboard. Whatever they type is stored in a special variable called answer.

Because answer changes every time someone types, it is a good idea to copy it into a variable with a meaningful name:

Storing user input in a well-named variable

Trace the result. If the user types Maya, the value Maya is stored in answer, and then copied into the variable Name. Now, even if the user later types something else, the variable Name still remembers Maya.

Now Sami builds a calculator in Scratch. It has an addition button and a subtraction button, each a sprite. Here is the working code:

Scratch: a calculator that adds or subtracts two user inputs

--- Subtraction button sprite ---

Trace the result. Suppose the user clicks the addition button and enters 7 then 5. Number1 becomes 7, Number2 becomes 5, Result becomes 7 + 5 = 12, and the sprite says 12. If instead the user clicks the subtraction button and enters 7 then 5, Result becomes 7 - 5 = 2, and the sprite says 2. The calculation blocks use the arithmetic operators + and - from the green Operators section.

Comparison operators and conditions

Sometimes we want to compare two values rather than do maths with them. A comparison operator compares two values and gives back True or False. In programming we say it returns True or False. The one you need here is equal to, written =. It checks if two values are the same.

Imagine a ride at a theme park where you must be exactly 150 cm tall. If your height is 150, then Height = 150 returns True. If your height is 160, then Height = 150 returns False, because 160 is not the same as 150.

A comparison like this is called a condition. A condition is like a question that can only be answered True or False. Height = 150 can be read as the question: 'Is height equal to 150?' Conditions are the foundation of selection, which is the very next subunit.
concept-2-using-operators.example: Computers often use the equal to operator to check passwords: they compare what you type with the stored password. A strong password is long and easy for you to remember — three random words such as riverlemontiger work well. Never write your password down where others can see it, and never share it with anyone.

concept-3-selection.explanation:
So far your programs have run in a straight line — every instruction, every time. Selection changes that. Selection lets your program decide what to do next, based on the answer to a condition. It is the third big way to control a program, alongside sequence (the order of instructions) and iteration (repeating instructions).

A selection statement has a condition and some instructions that run only if the condition is True. We write it with IF, THEN and ELSE. After IF comes the condition. After THEN comes what to do if the condition is True. After ELSE comes what to do if the condition is False.

An everyday IF THEN ELSE selection statement

Continue with the rest of the day

Trace the result. If it is very cold, the condition is True, so you take a jacket. If it is not very cold, the condition is False, so you take a jumper instead. Either way, you then continue with the rest of your day. If there were no ELSE, then when the condition was False the program would simply skip the jacket step and carry on.

Here is another example. Notice that the last line runs no matter what:

Only one of the first two lines runs; the last line always runs

Trace the result. If it is the morning, the program says 'Good morning'. If it is not, it says 'Good afternoon'. In both cases it then says 'How are you?', because that instruction is outside the selection statement.

In Scratch, selection uses the if <> then block and the if <> then ... else block from the orange Control section. The diamond-and-hexagon shape at the top holds the condition. Here is a program that reacts to the colour of your T-shirt:

Scratch: selection that checks user input

Trace the result. If the user types blue, the condition TShirtColour = blue is True, so the sprite switches to the blue costume. If the user types anything else, the condition is False, so the ELSE branch runs and the sprite switches to the orange costume.

concept-4-planning-solutions.explanation:
Good programmers plan before they build. In this subunit you learn that the same task can be solved by different algorithms, that some algorithms are more efficient than others, and how to plan a solution by breaking a problem into parts.

Different algorithms, different efficiency

Think about walking from your classroom to the lunch hall. There are several routes, and some are shorter than others. In the same way, one problem can be solved by several algorithms. An algorithm is efficient when it carries out only the instructions that are actually needed, with no wasted steps.

One great way to make an algorithm more efficient is to use selection to skip steps you do not need. Compare two versions of a morning routine:

A linear routine versus a routine that uses selection

3 IF ShoweredLastNight equal to YES

6 Take a shower, then get dressed

7 Eat breakfast, then brush your teeth

Trace the result. The linear routine always does all 7 steps, even on a day you already showered last night, and even on a weekend. The selection routine checks conditions first: if you showered last night, it skips the shower; if it is not a school day, it does not send you to school. Even though the selection version is longer to write, it is more efficient to run, because it does not do unnecessary work.

Decomposition means breaking a big problem into smaller parts, called sub-problems, that are easier to solve one at a time. When we plan a program, it helps to decompose the problem into four things a computer can work with: inputs, processes, conditions and outputs.

Maya plans a small chatbot that asks about a favourite animal. If you answer 'panda', it agrees with you; otherwise it gently disagrees. First she decomposes the problem into its parts:

Input: ask the user for their favourite animal and store the answer.

Process: keep the answer in a variable called FavouriteAnimal.

Condition: check IF FavouriteAnimal is equal to panda.

Output: say one message if True, and a different message if False.

Then she turns her plan into an algorithm, and finally into Scratch code:

Scratch: a chatbot planned by decomposition

say [That is a cool animal, but pandas are the best!] for 2 seconds

Trace the result. If the user types panda, the condition is True and the chatbot says 'Mine too!'. If the user types lion (or anything else), the condition is False and it says 'That is a cool animal, but pandas are the best!'. Because Maya planned the input, process, condition and output first, building the code was quick and clear.

Programmers use comments to explain their code. In an algorithm we often write a comment after two slashes, like this: // this line checks the answer. Comments do not run — they are just notes for humans to read. They make a program much friendlier to work on.

Part — What it means · Example

Input — Data the user gives to the program. · The user types their answer.

Process — The work the program does with the data. · The answer is stored in a variable.

Condition — A True/False question the program checks. · Is the answer equal to 'panda'?

concept-5-object-interaction.explanation:
In computing, an object is a thing that has its own shape and its own behaviours. Look around your room: a book is an object (it is made of paper, has text, and can be opened and closed); a learner is an object (they wear a uniform and can read and write). In Scratch, the objects are the sprites and the stage. Sprites can change how they look using costumes, and we program their behaviour using scripts.

A script is a set of joined blocks that makes one complete section of a program. A trigger tells a script when to run — for example, when green flag clicked or when this sprite clicked. A sub-routine is a named set of instructions that does one particular job. You define a sub-routine (write its instructions), and it only runs when you call it. In Scratch, one common way to make a sub-routine is with the broadcast block, which sends a message, and a when I receive block that catches the message and runs the sub-routine.

An interaction is when two or more objects communicate or work together. Think of a relay race: each runner is an object with their own behaviours, and they are interrelated because the next runner can only take the baton once the previous runner passes it. The action of one object affects another. In a game, if a player object passes a ball, the ball object must move — so the two objects are interrelated, and we write a sub-routine for each.

Theo builds a game with three objects: the rocket ship, an asteroid, and the stage. The player moves the rocket up and down to dodge asteroids that fly in from the right. Let us look at each object's script.

The rocket ship uses selection to move, and it has two sub-routines (called by broadcasts) for when it is hit and when the game is over:

Scratch: the rocket ship object with two sub-routines

--- Rocket ship: main script ---

--- Rocket ship: 'Hit' sub-routine ---

--- Rocket ship: 'GameOver' sub-routine ---

The asteroid object flies across the screen. It changes the score when the rocket dodges it, and it broadcasts 'Hit' if it touches the rocket:

Scratch: the asteroid object that interacts with the rocket ship

The stage object ends the game when the lives run out:

Scratch: the stage object that ends the game

Trace the result. The asteroid starts at the right edge at a random height and moves left. While it moves, it keeps checking touching Rocket ship?. If it touches, Lives goes down by 1 and it broadcasts 'Hit', so the rocket's Hit sub-routine says 'Ouch!' and flashes a colour. Straight after a hit, the asteroid waits half a second and jumps back to the right edge, so a single bump costs exactly one life instead of draining every life while the two objects are still overlapping. If the asteroid crosses the whole screen without touching, Score goes up by 1. When Lives reaches 0, the stage switches to the Game Over backdrop, broadcasts 'GameOver' (so the rocket explodes and says 'Game over!'), and stop all halts every script. The rocket, asteroid and stage all interact through the shared variables Lives and Score and the broadcast messages.

concept-6-creating-user-friendly-program.explanation:
A program is user-friendly when people can use it easily and enjoy using it. Big programs are made by whole teams, each person with a different job. In this subunit you learn the roles people play, the stages a program goes through, and why you must agree on clear criteria at the start.

Turning a good idea into a finished program takes people with many different skills. Here are the main roles:

Making a program can be decomposed into five stages, called the project life cycle. It is called a cycle because there is no fixed end: even a finished program can be analysed again and improved.

Analysis — study the problem, come up with an idea, and decide the criteria and main features.

Design — plan what the program will look like and how it will work; draw the screens and write the algorithms.

Development — build the program by writing the code, and create the content such as text, images and sounds.

Testing — run the program and check it works against the success criteria; fix anything that does not work.

Evaluation — judge the quality of the program by checking its features against the original criteria.

E-waste is waste from old electronic devices. The World Economic Forum says there could be about 74.7 million tonnes of e-waste each year by 2030 — about the same weight as 10 million elephants! One way to help is to reuse and recycle devices instead of always buying new ones.

Criteria are the standards you use to judge if a program is successful. Success criteria need to be specific and measurable so anyone can check whether they have been met. Imagine being asked to build a quiz with no criteria — how would you know if it was good? It is far better to agree the criteria at the analysis stage, by asking questions such as: How many questions should the quiz have? What happens if the user gets a question right? What happens if they get it wrong?

Maya builds a quiz program and evaluates it against clear criteria. Here is her first question, written correctly in Scratch:

Scratch: one user-friendly quiz question with a clear right/wrong response

ask [What do you use to store values that can change in a program?] and wait

Trace the result. The quiz greets the user, then asks the question. If the user types variable, the score goes up by 1 and it says 'That is correct!'. If they type anything else, it says 'Oh no. The correct answer is: variable'. At the end it shows the score. This meets several success criteria at once: it asks a programming question, it responds differently to right and wrong answers, and it shows the final score. To add more questions, Maya duplicates the IF ELSE block and edits the question, answer and messages.

Role — What they do

End user — The person the program is made for, who will use it when it is finished.

Analyst — Interviews the end user to understand their needs, and helps create the criteria.

UX designer — Designs the menus, buttons and layout so the program is easy to use.

Content creator — Makes the text, images, sounds and other content in the program.

Graphic designer — Creates the digital images and visual look using design software.

Software developer — Plans the solution with algorithms, then writes the code.

Product tester — Uses the program a lot to find problems so they can be fixed.

concept-7-using-selection-with-a-physica.explanation:
Now for something different: a physical device — a small computer you could hold in your hand and program yourself. We use the BBC micro:bit. It has inputs (button A, button B, and a sensor that feels movement) and outputs (a grid of 25 red LED lights and a tiny speaker). In this subunit you use conditions and selection to make the micro:bit respond to what the user does.

You do NOT need to own a micro:bit

Go to makecode.microbit.org for blocks, or python.microbit.org for Python. A picture of a micro:bit (the simulator) appears on the screen. When you run your code, the simulator behaves exactly like a real micro:bit — you can click its A and B buttons with your mouse, and press a shake button to shake it. Everything in this subunit works in the free online simulator alone.

Variables and conditions on the micro:bit

Just like in Scratch, you make a variable in MakeCode by clicking Variables, then Make a Variable. You can set it and change it. The micro:bit also has ready-made conditions for checking inputs — for example, button A is pressed and is [shake] gesture. These conditions return True or False, so you can use them with selection.

A gesture is a movement the micro:bit can feel, such as being shaken. Here is a program that shows a different face depending on whether it is being shaken. In MakeCode blocks it looks like this:

MakeCode: selection using the shake gesture condition

Trace the result. The forever loop keeps checking the condition. While the micro:bit is being shaken, the condition is True, so it shows a sad face. When it is still, the condition is False, so it shows a happy face.

Now build a counter. Each press of button A adds 1; each press of button B subtracts 1; shaking resets it to 0. We use on button A pressed and on button B pressed, which run exactly once each time you press. Here it is in MakeCode blocks:

MakeCode: a counter using inputs, a variable and selection

The very same program can be written in MicroPython at python.microbit.org. This is real text code that runs on the simulator:

Trace the result. Count starts at 0. Press button A three times and Count becomes 3, shown on the LED screen. Press button B once and it drops to 2. Shake the micro:bit and Count is reset to 0 and the screen is cleared. This program uses an input (the buttons and the shake), a variable (Count), selection (checking which input happened), and produces an output (the number on the screen).

The two-player 'Guess the Press' game

For the club's final micro:bit challenge, everyone builds a two-player game. Player one presses button A a secret number of times. Player two then presses button B, trying to guess and match that number. When the micro:bit is shaken, the two numbers are compared: if they are equal, a smiley face shows; if not, a sad face shows. Here it is in MakeCode:

MakeCode: the two-player Guess the Press game

And here is the same game in MicroPython:

The same Guess the Press game in MicroPython

When the micro:bit is shaken, the condition PlayerOne = PlayerTwo is True, so a happy face shows. If player two had pressed B only three times, the condition would be False and a sad face would show. After a short pause, both variables reset to 0 and the screen clears, ready for another round. This one small game uses variables, inputs, the equal to operator, and IF THEN ELSE selection — almost everything from the whole unit!

concept-2-data-and-information-are-not-t.explanation:
Here is an idea that many people get muddled, so read it slowly. Data is meaningless facts or figures on their own, like the number 7 or the word green. By itself, green does not tell you anything useful. Information is data that has been given meaning. When we say 'green is the most popular colour in the class', that is information, because now the fact means something. Managing data well is really the art of turning plain data into useful information.

Here is the key difference to remember. Discrete data is counted and is always a whole value — you cannot have half a pet or three-and-a-bit customers. Continuous data is measured and can be any value at all, like a temperature of 24.5 degrees or a height of 1.42 metres. In Leila's fruit investigation, the type of fruit ('mango', 'banana') is categorical, and the number of learners who chose each fruit is discrete. In Zane's temperature investigation, each reading is continuous.

Before you collect a single number, ask yourself four planning questions. Answering them first saves you a lot of trouble later.

What data do I want to collect? For example, 'the favourite fruit of each learner in my class'.

How will I collect the data? With a form, a data logger, a survey, or a spreadsheet.

How will I organise the data? Usually by putting it into a spreadsheet in a sensible order.

concept-3-the-tools-we-use-to-collect-an.explanation:
Humans are not very good at collecting and organising lots of data by hand — we forget things, make mistakes, and it takes ages. Computers are far better: they do not forget, and they measure and calculate very quickly. Here are the most useful computing tools for a statistical investigation.

Data loggers — a data logger is a device that reads and records data from the world automatically (by itself, with no human help) and continuously (carrying on until you tell it to stop). It uses sensors. For example, a data logger could record the temperature of a fish tank every five minutes, all day and night. Data loggers are excellent for collecting continuous data like temperature, light level or a person's pulse.

Spreadsheets — such as LibreOffice Calc. A spreadsheet stores data in a neat grid of cells, and it can add up columns, do other calculations, and draw charts in an instant. It is designed to make working with numbers easy.

Databases — a database stores related data of many types (not just numbers) in an organised way. It can be paper-based, like a diary or calendar, or digital. Databases make it easy to find, sort and analyse data, and they can hold enormous amounts — far more than a spreadsheet.

Forms — a form is a list of questions with spaces for people to mark or write their answers. A good form makes people enter their data in the same way, so it is easy to organise. Forms can be on paper or on a screen.

Document production tools — word processors and presentation programs let you put text and pictures together to make a report or a presentation, which is a good way to share the results of your investigation.

A data logger works day and night without ever getting tired or bored.

Scientists put data loggers in places no human could stay, like the top of a mountain or the bottom of the sea, and leave them for months to record the temperature or the weather all by themselves.

Some hotels use data loggers in a control system: when the temperature reaches 23 degrees a cooling system switches on by itself, and if it falls to 18 degrees the heating turns on.

Let us help Leila. Her question is, 'What is the favourite fruit in my class?' She designs a simple form with one clear question — 'What is your favourite fruit?' — and a list of choices to tick: Mango, Banana, Orange, Watermelon, Dates, and a space for 'other'. Giving people a list of choices is clever, because it stops one person writing 'mango', another writing 'Mangoes' and another writing 'MANGO' — which would be three different answers to the computer, even though they mean the same fruit.

After every classmate has filled in the form, Leila counts up the answers and stores them in a LibreOffice Calc spreadsheet. She organises the data in two columns — the fruit, and the number of learners who chose it — and sorts it from most popular to least popular:

concept-5-restricting-cells.explanation:
It is very easy to enter data incorrectly. If Zara typed a birthday as 3112 instead of 31/12, she would never find that birthday again when she searched. If Karim typed ouzzle instead of puzzle, the spreadsheet would treat it as a different word. Validation rules limit the kind of data a cell will accept, and this stops many of these mistakes before they happen. In LibreOffice Calc you set them with Data > Validity. A cell can be made to accept:

only decimal numbers, for example a temperature;

only text from a list you provide, like a drop-down of Yes and No;

only numbers between two limits, for example a score from 1 to 5 (so the cell would refuse a 6).

Imagine Zane is scoring the school lunch out of 5. He selects the score column, opens Data > Validity, sets Allow to Whole Numbers, the condition to between, Minimum 1 and Maximum 5. On the Error Alert tab he chooses the Stop action. Now the cell politely refuses any score below 1 or above 5, and even refuses a word — so his data stays clean and correct.

Type of data — What it is · Examples · Row · A · B

Categorical — Data that can be grouped into categories. It is often made of words. · Favourite colour, type of pet, book titles, people's names. · 1 · Fruit · Number of learners

Discrete — Numerical data that can only be certain values, usually whole numbers you count. · Number of learners, number of customer reviews, number of pets. · 2 · Mango · 9

concept-6-representing-data.explanation:
Once you have collected some data, you can represent it — that is, show it — in different ways. A good representation makes the meaning of the data leap out at you. In this subunit you will learn to represent data in tables, bar charts and line graphs, and you will learn to calculate with formulas and functions in LibreOffice Calc.

The simplest way to represent data is in a table of rows and columns, exactly like a spreadsheet. A table makes it easy to see which pieces of data go together. Here is a table Leila made about how the 24 learners in her class travel to school:

By reading the table we get information: most learners walk to school, and very few come by car. If we add up the numbers 12 + 9 + 3 we get 24, the whole class. Because 12 is half of 24, we can even say that half the class walks to school. A table like this is much easier to read than the same facts written out in a long sentence.

But a table is not always enough. Imagine a table showing the eye colour of everyone in a big city, with numbers like 252780, 344700 and 574500. Those numbers are so big that it is hard to get a clear picture of which is largest. This is exactly when a chart becomes useful.

concept-7-bar-charts.explanation:
A bar chart has a separate coloured bar for each category. The longer the bar, the greater the value. Because bar charts work by counting how many times each option is chosen, they are perfect for categorical data (like favourite fruit) and discrete data (like a number of votes). Here is Leila's fruit data again, ready to become a bar chart:

On the bar chart, mango would have the tallest bar and dates the shortest. You can see the winner in a single glance, without reading any numbers at all. To make this chart in LibreOffice Calc, Leila follows these steps:

Select the data, including the headings: click and drag across the Fruit column and the Number column together.

Open the menu Insert > Chart. The Chart Wizard appears.

In Step 1 — Choose a Chart Type, pick Column for bars that stand up tall (or Bar for bars that lie sideways). Click Next.

In Steps 2 and 3, make sure 'First row as label' and 'First column as label' are ticked, then click Next.

In Step 4 — Chart Elements, type a clear Title such as 'Favourite fruit in our class', label the axes, and tick Display legend. Click Finish.

Click anywhere outside the chart to leave edit mode. Your bar chart is done!

More than half of all the people in the world have brown eyes — that is around 4 billion people!

concept-8-the-parts-of-a-chart.explanation:
Bar charts and line graphs have two lines called axes. The y axis goes up and down (it is vertical) and usually shows the scale, like the number of learners. The x axis goes from side to side (it is horizontal) and usually shows the categories or the time. The title you put on each axis is called a label, and labels explain what each axis measures. The little key that tells you what each colour means is called the legend. A chart without labels is like a letter with no address — nobody can be sure what it means.

Bar charts can be drawn two ways. A column chart has vertical bars going up; a bar chart in LibreOffice has horizontal bars going across. Both show the same information — you simply choose whichever is easier to read.

Line graphs: for continuous data

A line graph is best for continuous data that changes over time, because the sloping lines show you how the data rises and falls between the points. Let us help Zane. He set up a data logger to record the temperature in his Mogadishu classroom every hour. This is his data:

To draw this by hand, you would mark a dot for each temperature at the right height above its time, then join the dots with straight lines. LibreOffice Calc does it for you: select the data, choose Insert > Chart, and pick the Line chart type in the wizard. The finished line climbs from the cool early morning up to a peak at 32 degrees at 1 o'clock, then slopes back down as the afternoon cools. The shape of the line tells the story instantly, which is why Zane chooses the club's outdoor games for the cooler early morning. This temperature data is a perfect example of continuous data.

Why not use a bar chart for this? Because temperature flows smoothly from one reading to the next, and the lines show that flow. And why not use a line graph for favourite fruit? Because the fruits are separate categories, not a smooth change over time — joining 'mango' to 'banana' with a line would make no sense at all. Choosing the right chart is a real skill.

Sometimes you make a chart and then realise a different kind would be clearer. Happily, this is easy to change in LibreOffice Calc: double-click the chart to enter edit mode, then right-click it and choose Chart Type, pick Line (or Column), and click OK. Click outside to finish. You can also change the style and labels to suit who will read the chart. Good choices matter:

For a reader who is colour-blind and cannot tell red from green, choose different colours (like blue and orange) or add clear labels to each line, so the colours are not the only clue.

For a chart shown on a small screen, keep it simple: a summary with big, clear text.

For a chart shown on a big screen to a whole room, you can show lots of detail and many data points.

You can change the title, the axis labels, the gridlines, the colours and the size of the text to make any chart clearer.

A spreadsheet is also a brilliant calculator. In maths you already use operators — the symbols for calculations. In a spreadsheet, some of the symbols are different, so learn these four carefully:

The two to watch are multiply and divide. On paper you write 6 x 4, but in a spreadsheet you type an asterisk: =6*4, which returns 24. On paper you write a division sign, but in a spreadsheet you type a forward slash: =20/4, which returns 5.
concept-8-the-parts-of-a-chart.example: A formula is an instruction to do a calculation, and in a spreadsheet a formula must always begin with an equals sign =. The = tells LibreOffice Calc, 'Do not treat this as ordinary text — work it out for me.' The real magic is that instead of typing a number in a formula, you usually type a cell reference — the address of the cell where that number lives, like A1 or B3. Look at this tiny example:

concept-9-a-formula-that-uses-cell-refer.explanation:
The formula =A1+A2 means 'the value in cell A1 plus the value in cell A2'. It shows 9. Here is the clever part: if you later change A1 from 3 to 5, the result in A3 updates all by itself to 11. You never have to work it out again. Because of this, always put a formula in a cell of its own, not in one of the cells you are calculating with.

Sometimes a formula would be very long. Imagine adding up twenty test scores with + signs — it would take ages and be easy to get wrong. That is why spreadsheets have functions: ready-made calculations built into the software. To use one, type =, then the function name, then the cell range in brackets. A range is all the cells between and including two cells, written with a colon : that means 'to'. So B2:B6 means every cell from B2 to B6. The two functions you will use most are:

The two functions you will use most

=SUM(B2:B6) adds up every value from B2 to B6

=AVERAGE(B2:B6) finds the average (mean) of every value from B2 to B6

concept-10-worked-example-ehel-academy-t.explanation:
The class has done three maths tests this term, each marked out of 10. Their teacher types the marks into LibreOffice Calc and wants to work out each learner's total and percentage, and the total and average for each test. Here is the data:

First, the total for each learner. In cell E2 you type =B2+C2+D2 and press Enter; it shows 24, because 8 + 7 + 9 = 24. You can copy this formula down to E6 (select E2 and press Ctrl+D, or drag the little handle at the corner of the cell). LibreOffice cleverly changes the row numbers for you, so E3 becomes =B3+C3+D3. Here are all the totals:

Column E: each learner's total out of 30

Next, the percentage. Each learner could score 30 in total (10 on each of the three tests), so the percentage is the total divided by 30. In cell F2 you type =E2/30. This shows 0.8 at first, because 24 divided by 30 is 0.8. To make it look like a percentage, keep F2 selected and click the percentage button (marked %) on the Formatting toolbar. Now it shows 80.00%. Leila scored 80%. Nora scored 28/30, which is 0.9333..., or 93.33% — and that is why some percentages have decimal places, because 28 does not divide evenly by 30.

concept-11-average-of-test-1.explanation:
Average of Test 2: in C8 type =AVERAGE(C2:C6) -> 8

Average of Test 3: in D8 type =AVERAGE(D2:D6) -> 8.2

Let us check by hand so you can see the software is right. Test 1 scores are 8, 6, 9, 7 and 10, which add up to 40; divide by the 5 learners and the average is 8. Test 3 scores are 9, 7, 8, 8 and 9, which add up to 41; divide by 5 and the average is 8.2. The .2 is a decimal because 41 does not divide evenly by 5 — this is completely normal for an average. Everything the spreadsheet worked out matches our pencil-and-paper check.

A single LibreOffice Calc spreadsheet has 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns.

That is more than 17 billion cells in one sheet — far more than anyone could ever fill by hand.

Calc also has more than 500 ready-made functions waiting for you, though SUM and AVERAGE are the two you will use most this year.

concept-12-using-data.example: Sometimes we need to change the data in a spreadsheet — maybe we spot a mistake, or we get new information, or a price changes. Spreadsheets are very clever about this. When you change a piece of data, every formula and every chart that uses that data updates instantly, all by itself. You never have to redo your calculations or redraw your charts by hand.

concept-13-worked-example-aunt-nora-s-ju.example: Now watch what happens when data changes. Nora realises she forgot to count 5 customers who came in on Monday while she stepped out — there were really 30, not 25. She clicks cell B4, types 30, and presses Enter. Instantly, two things update by themselves:

concept-14-changing-one-cell-updates-eve.explanation:
Before: B4 = 25 -> D4 =C4/B4 = 150000 / 25 = 6000

After: B4 = 30 -> D4 =C4/B4 = 150000 / 30 = 5000

The weekly total customers =SUM(B2:B8) changes from 255 to 260.

The average spend for Monday drops from 6000 to 5000 shillings, and the weekly customer total rises from 255 to 260. But notice that the takings in cell C4 stayed exactly the same at 150000. Why? Because C4 holds a number that Nora typed in herself, not a formula — so nothing told it to change. Only cells with a formula recalculate. This is an important idea: typed values stay put, but formulas react to change.

The very same thing happens to charts. If Nora had made a bar chart of her daily customers, the Monday bar would have grown taller by itself the moment she changed 25 to 30. She never has to touch the chart. This is why spreadsheets are so powerful for a shop owner: she can try out a change and see the effect on all her totals and charts in a single second.

Spreadsheets often hold a great deal of data, and it is slow to find one thing by reading every row. Instead we use search criteria — the words or conditions we search for to find data that matches. You already use search criteria every time you type words into a search engine on the internet. Shops do this too: a supermarket can search its records for every customer who often buys dates, and then send just those customers a special offer on dates.
