we02.solution:
Here is an idea that many people get muddled, so read it slowly. Data is meaningless facts or figures on their own, like the number 7 or the word green. By itself, green does not tell you anything useful. Information is data that has been given meaning. When we say 'green is the most popular colour in the class', that is information, because now the fact means something. Managing data well is really the art of turning plain data into useful information.

Here is the key difference to remember. Discrete data is counted and is always a whole value — you cannot have half a pet or three-and-a-bit customers. Continuous data is measured and can be any value at all, like a temperature of 24.5 degrees or a height of 1.42 metres. In Leila's fruit investigation, the type of fruit ('mango', 'banana') is categorical, and the number of learners who chose each fruit is discrete. In Zane's temperature investigation, each reading is continuous.

Before you collect a single number, ask yourself four planning questions. Answering them first saves you a lot of trouble later.

What data do I want to collect? For example, 'the favourite fruit of each learner in my class'.

How will I collect the data? With a form, a data logger, a survey, or a spreadsheet.

How will I organise the data? Usually by putting it into a spreadsheet in a sensible order.

For example: How will I use the data to get information? Perhaps by counting, calculating, and drawing a chart to make the pattern clear.

we03.solution:
Humans are not very good at collecting and organising lots of data by hand — we forget things, make mistakes, and it takes ages. Computers are far better: they do not forget, and they measure and calculate very quickly. Here are the most useful computing tools for a statistical investigation.

Data loggers — a data logger is a device that reads and records data from the world automatically (by itself, with no human help) and continuously (carrying on until you tell it to stop). It uses sensors. For example, a data logger could record the temperature of a fish tank every five minutes, all day and night. Data loggers are excellent for collecting continuous data like temperature, light level or a person's pulse.

Spreadsheets — such as LibreOffice Calc. A spreadsheet stores data in a neat grid of cells, and it can add up columns, do other calculations, and draw charts in an instant. It is designed to make working with numbers easy.

Databases — a database stores related data of many types (not just numbers) in an organised way. It can be paper-based, like a diary or calendar, or digital. Databases make it easy to find, sort and analyse data, and they can hold enormous amounts — far more than a spreadsheet.

Forms — a form is a list of questions with spaces for people to mark or write their answers. A good form makes people enter their data in the same way, so it is easy to organise. Forms can be on paper or on a screen.

Document production tools — word processors and presentation programs let you put text and pictures together to make a report or a presentation, which is a good way to share the results of your investigation.

A data logger works day and night without ever getting tired or bored.

Scientists put data loggers in places no human could stay, like the top of a mountain or the bottom of the sea, and leave them for months to record the temperature or the weather all by themselves.

Some hotels use data loggers in a control system: when the temperature reaches 23 degrees a cooling system switches on by itself, and if it falls to 18 degrees the heating turns on.

Let us help Leila. Her question is, 'What is the favourite fruit in my class?' She designs a simple form with one clear question — 'What is your favourite fruit?' — and a list of choices to tick: Mango, Banana, Orange, Watermelon, Dates, and a space for 'other'. Giving people a list of choices is clever, because it stops one person writing 'mango', another writing 'Mangoes' and another writing 'MANGO' — which would be three different answers to the computer, even though they mean the same fruit.

After every classmate has filled in the form, Leila counts up the answers and stores them in a LibreOffice Calc spreadsheet. She organises the data in two columns — the fruit, and the number of learners who chose it — and sorts it from most popular to least popular:

For example: Now the data has become information. Leila can see straight away that mango is the favourite fruit in her class, chosen by 9 learners, and that dates were chosen by the fewest. The type of fruit is categorical data, and the number of learners who chose each fruit is discrete data. If Leila adds up the numbers 9 + 6 + 4 + 4 + 2, she finds that 25 learners answered her form altogether.

we05.solution:
It is very easy to enter data incorrectly. If Zara typed a birthday as 3112 instead of 31/12, she would never find that birthday again when she searched. If Karim typed ouzzle instead of puzzle, the spreadsheet would treat it as a different word. Validation rules limit the kind of data a cell will accept, and this stops many of these mistakes before they happen. In LibreOffice Calc you set them with Data > Validity. A cell can be made to accept:

only decimal numbers, for example a temperature;

only text from a list you provide, like a drop-down of Yes and No;

only numbers between two limits, for example a score from 1 to 5 (so the cell would refuse a 6).

Imagine Zane is scoring the school lunch out of 5. He selects the score column, opens Data > Validity, sets Allow to Whole Numbers, the condition to between, Minimum 1 and Maximum 5. On the Error Alert tab he chooses the Stop action. Now the cell politely refuses any score below 1 or above 5, and even refuses a word — so his data stays clean and correct.

Type of data — What it is · Examples · Row · A · B

Categorical — Data that can be grouped into categories. It is often made of words. · Favourite colour, type of pet, book titles, people's names. · 1 · Fruit · Number of learners

Discrete — Numerical data that can only be certain values, usually whole numbers you count. · Number of learners, number of customer reviews, number of pets. · 2 · Mango · 9

For example: Continuous — Numerical data that can take ANY value in a range, usually measured, not counted. · Temperature, weight, height, length, the time taken to do something. · 3 · Banana · 6

we06.solution:
Once you have collected some data, you can represent it — that is, show it — in different ways. A good representation makes the meaning of the data leap out at you. In this subunit you will learn to represent data in tables, bar charts and line graphs, and you will learn to calculate with formulas and functions in LibreOffice Calc.

The simplest way to represent data is in a table of rows and columns, exactly like a spreadsheet. A table makes it easy to see which pieces of data go together. Here is a table Leila made about how the 24 learners in her class travel to school:

By reading the table we get information: most learners walk to school, and very few come by car. If we add up the numbers 12 + 9 + 3 we get 24, the whole class. Because 12 is half of 24, we can even say that half the class walks to school. A table like this is much easier to read than the same facts written out in a long sentence.

But a table is not always enough. Imagine a table showing the eye colour of everyone in a big city, with numbers like 252780, 344700 and 574500. Those numbers are so big that it is hard to get a clear picture of which is largest. This is exactly when a chart becomes useful.

For example: A chart (or graph) is like a picture of your data. Charts make it much quicker and easier to see patterns and to summarise information. There are several kinds, and a good data manager chooses the kind that best suits the data. The two you will use most are the bar chart and the line graph.

rule-7.text: Every formula must start with an equals sign. No equals sign, no calculation! In a spreadsheet, * means multiply and / means divide. Use a cell reference (like B3) in a formula, and the answer updates by itself when that cell changes. Calculations using functions: SUM and AVERAGE Sometimes a formula would be very long. Imagine adding up twenty test scores with + signs — it would take ages and be easy to get wrong. That is why spreadsheets have functions: ready-made calculations built into the software. To use one, type =, then the function name, then the cell range in brackets. A range is all the cells between and including two cells, written with a colon : that means 'to'. rule-8.text: Change one cell, and every formula and chart that uses it updates by itself, instantly. A cell with a formula recalculates; a cell with a typed-in value does not change on its own. This is why we use cell references in formulas instead of typing the numbers straight in. Finding specific data with search criteria Spreadsheets often hold a great deal of data, and it is slow to find one thing by reading every row. Instead we use search criteria — the words or conditions we search for to find data that matches. You already use search criteria every time you type words into a search engine on the internet. Shops do this too: a supermarket can search its records for every customer who often buys dates, and then send just those customers a special offer on dates. concept-1-network-hardware-the-machines-.explanation:
Computers can only share files, printers and software if they are joined together into a network. Think of a network like a group of friends who can all talk to each other. On its own, one computer is like a person standing alone in a room. Connect it to a network and suddenly it can talk to every other device — sharing photos, sending messages, and reaching the whole internet.

There are two ways a device can join a network: with wires, or without wires (wirelessly). Both work well, but each needs different hardware. Hardware means the real, physical machines you could hold in your hand — as opposed to software, which is the programs that run on them. In this part you will meet three key pieces of network hardware.

Connecting with wires: the Ethernet cable

Many devices connect to a network using an Ethernet cable. It looks a little like a thick telephone wire with a clip on the end that clicks into a socket. Wired connections are fast and reliable, but the device cannot move far because it is tied to the cable. Two important devices use these cables to build a network: the switch and the router. They have lots of sockets, so many cables (and therefore many devices) can plug into them at once.

The switch — a meeting point for wired devices

A switch lets you connect wired devices together on one network, such as your school network or an office network. You can plug in many devices, for example:

The switch joins all these devices together so they can communicate — that is, send data to and receive data from each other. Here is the clever part: if you connect a single printer to the switch, then every computer on that network can use that one printer. The switch is like a busy meeting point where all the wired devices come together to talk. On its own, though, a switch cannot reach the internet — it only connects devices that are on the same network.

The router — the doorway to the internet

A router does something different. It lets different networks talk to each other. Its most common job is to connect a small network — like your home or school — to the huge network we call the internet.

For example, a router connects Ehel Academy's network to the internet. Because of the router, any device on the school network can reach the internet — so a student can open a website, watch a lesson video, or send a message to a cousin far away. If you remember only one thing, remember this: it is the router — and only the router — that lets devices on your network reach other networks and the internet.

Connecting without wires: the wireless access point

A wired switch and a wireless access point do a similar job — they both let computers join a network. The big difference is that the wireless access point needs no cables. Devices connect to it through the air. This is perfect for devices that move around, such as:

The most common wireless access point is a Wi-Fi access point. It sends and receives signals — special invisible waves that carry data through the air to and from nearby devices. A huge advantage is that hundreds of devices can connect to a single Wi-Fi access point without any wires at all. Compare that to a wired switch, which needs one separate cable for every single device!

Wi-Fi signals only travel a short distance, though. The further you walk away from the access point, the weaker the signal becomes — until, eventually, your device drops off the network. That is why Wi-Fi access points are often fixed high up on walls or ceilings, sometimes with an aerial sticking out. An aerial is the part that helps send and receive the signals.

How is a wireless access point different from a switch?

If you put a switch and a Wi-Fi access point side by side, the biggest difference is simple: the switch uses cables, while the wireless access point uses signals through the air. A switch is best for devices that stay still, like a desktop computer or a printer. A wireless access point is best for devices you carry around, like a phone or a tablet. Both connect devices to the same network — they just do it in different ways.

Here is how the three devices fit together in a typical network. Read the diagram below from top to bottom — the internet is at the top, and the devices are at the bottom:

A simple network: the router reaches the internet; the switch connects wired devices; the wireless access point connects devices with no wires.

+-----------+ +--------------------+

+-----------+ +--------------------+

In many homes there is just ONE box that plugs into the wall — people call it 'the Wi-Fi' or 'the router'. But that single box is actually doing three jobs at once! Inside it there is a router, a switch, AND a wireless access point, all built together. In a big school or office, these three are often separate machines so they can handle many more devices.

"Give me a device — like a printer, a phone or a smart TV — and ask me whether it would connect to the network through the switch, the wireless access point, or the router. Then tell me if I was right and explain why."

This turns your tutor into a quiz partner and helps the three devices stick in your memory.

concept-2-how-data-travels-through-netwo.explanation:
You now know the hardware that joins devices together. But how does a message actually travel from your device, across the world, and arrive at exactly the right computer? That is the amazing journey you will follow in this part.

Cellular networks: the internet almost anywhere

A cellular network is another kind of wireless network, but it works over very large areas. Instead of a small Wi-Fi box on a wall, cellular networks use tall towers (you may have seen them standing high above towns and along roads). These towers send out strong signals that a smartphone can pick up from many kilometres away.

A single cell tower can reach a phone up to about 50 kilometres away, although most of the time the useful range is around 5 kilometres. Making the towers tall is important, because it means the signal is less likely to be blocked by hills or buildings. This is why a mobile phone can connect almost anywhere — from the top of a mountain to the middle of a busy city. Some cars even use cellular networks, so they can download new software or let people make calls from inside the car.

Cellular networks have one big advantage: they cover enormous areas. But they share the same weakness as Wi-Fi — they can suffer from interference. Interference is anything that gets in the way of the signal, such as thick walls or bad weather. When there is interference, the signal may not reach your device properly. This can stop your phone from connecting, or make everything very slow.

concept-3-comparing-the-three-ways-to-co.explanation:
You have now met three ways for a device to connect: Wi-Fi, a wired Ethernet cable, and a cellular network (mobile data). Each one suits a different job. You would not want your phone tied to a wire while you walked around a city — and you would not use a slow, faraway cell tower to connect a printer that sits right next to your computer.

One way we compare connections is by their range — how far they reach. Another is their speed. Connection speed is measured in megabits per second, written Mbps. This is the fastest rate at which data can be sent. A higher number means data arrives more quickly, which matters a lot when you are streaming a video or downloading a big file.

IP addresses: every device has its own address

Think of the millions and millions of devices connected to the internet. When your device sends data, how does the internet know which of all those devices to deliver it to? The answer is that every device has its own unique address, called an IP address. IP stands for Internet Protocol.

An IP address is a set of numbers. A common type is made of four numbers separated by full stops, and each number is between 0 and 255. For example, a device might have the address 43.66.141.66. These numbers tell a computer exactly where to send data to, or where to fetch data from. IP addresses are usually created automatically by a small program, so you never have to type them yourself.

The best way to picture an IP address is to think of the address on a letter, or a post code. Every home has its own address so the postal worker knows exactly where to deliver each letter. In the same way, every device has its own IP address so the internet knows exactly where to deliver each piece of data. And just as no two homes on a street can share the same house number, no two devices on a network can share the same IP address — the automatic program makes sure each one is unique, so there is never any confusion.

There are two types of IP address. The older type is called IPv4 — and the world is starting to run OUT of IPv4 addresses, because there are so many devices! So a newer type was invented, called IPv6, which has an almost unlimited number of addresses — enough for every device for a very, very long time.

Here is one of the most surprising ideas about the internet. When you send a message or a photo, it does not travel as one big lump. Instead, before it is sent, the data is chopped up into many small chunks called packets. Packets are usually all about the same size.

Imagine Nadia in Hargeisa wants to send a message to Sami in Mogadishu. Her computer splits the message into, say, three packets. But each packet is not just a piece of the message — it also carries some extra labels. Every packet includes:

the IP address it was sent from (Nadia's device),

the IP address it is going to (Sami's device),

a packet number, so the pieces can be put back in the right order,

and, of course, a small piece of the actual message (the packet data).

Here is what one packet looks like inside. Notice the address labels at the top and the piece of data at the bottom:

One data packet. The 'sent from' and 'sent to' IP addresses are like the return address and destination address on an envelope.

+------------------------------------------+

+------------------------------------------+

concept-4-how-packets-travel-and-are-put.explanation:
When Nadia's packets set off across the internet, something interesting happens: they may take different routes to reach Sami. Just like cars driving from one city to another can take different roads, packets can travel by different paths. Some routes are quicker than others, so the packets often arrive in the wrong order!

This is not a problem, thanks to the packet number. When the packets arrive at their destination, Sami's computer reads the numbers and uses them to put the packets back into the correct order — like sorting shuffled pages of a story back to 1, 2, 3. Only once all the packets have arrived and are in order can the computer read the full message. Here is the whole journey in four steps:

What happens if a packet gets lost?

Sometimes a packet does not arrive at all — it gets lost along the way. When that happens, the internet has a neat way of fixing it:

The receiver computer notices a packet is missing, and sends a message back to the sender asking: "Please send packet 2 again, it got lost."

The sender computer sends another copy of just that one lost packet.

When the copy arrives, the receiver now has all the packets, so it puts them in order.

concept-6-advantages-and-disadvantages-o.explanation:
Splitting data into packets is a clever idea, and it brings real benefits — but it also has a few costs. It is important to understand both sides.

If a packet is lost, only a small piece of data has to be sent again — not the whole message.

Packets do not take up much bandwidth each, so they can travel along a greater variety of connections.

concept-7-how-websites-are-stored-and-ac.explanation:
You use websites every day — but where do they actually live? Every website is stored on a web server. A web server is a powerful computer that keeps all the pages of a website, along with the website's IP address, and it is always connected to the internet so people can reach it at any time.

So what happens when you visit a website? Imagine Sami types the address of Ehel Academy's website into his browser. Here is the journey of his request, step by step:

Sami types a web address into his web browser (a browser is a program such as Firefox). Another name for a web address is a URL — a Uniform Resource Locator. A URL is written as text, for example www.cambridge.org.

His web browser uses the internet to connect to the web server.

Because computers only really understand numbers, the URL is converted into an IP address behind the scenes.

The browser gives the web server that IP address, which tells it exactly where on the server the website is stored.

The web server checks the page is there, then sends the data back to the browser that asked for it — and the page appears on Sami's screen.

This explains a question you might have wondered about: why do we use words in web addresses when computers prefer numbers? The answer is that computers use IP addresses because they only understand numbers, but humans use URLs because words are far easier to remember than a long string of digits. Could you remember the number 93.184.216.34? Probably not — but you could easily remember a name like www.cambridge.org.

"All the packets of my message travel together in a neat line and arrive in order." Actually, no! Packets often split up, take different routes, and arrive jumbled and out of order. That is completely fine — each packet has a number, so the receiving computer sorts them back into the right order before reading the message.

When you visit websites, only use ones that you trust and know are safe. If you are not sure about a website, always check with your teacher, your parents, or a trusted adult BEFORE you visit it. Never type your name, address, school or password into a website you do not know.

concept-8-network-failure-when-connectio.explanation:
So far, everything has worked perfectly. But networks do not always behave. Cables get unplugged, power goes off, and sometimes whole services stop for hours. In this part you will find out what really happens when a network fails — and why, most of the time, you barely notice.

Let us be very clear about one word. A network is a collection of connections between devices. The internet is simply the biggest network of all — a massive, worldwide web of connections joining computers and devices everywhere. Every day, people all over the world use it for both work and fun. When you connect, you can reach all sorts of services stored on servers, such as:

cloud storage and online banking

holiday bookings and online shopping

messaging services, email and video calls
concept-8-network-failure-when-connectio.example: One of those services is cloud storage. Cloud storage lets you save your files and data on someone else's computer — usually a giant server owned by a big company. These companies have huge servers with enormous amounts of storage space, and they let you use some of it for your own files. The best part is that, because your files are stored on the internet, you can reach them from anywhere in the world — as long as you can connect to the internet. The word 'cloud' does not mean the sky; it just means 'stored on servers somewhere else, reached over the internet'.

Sometimes, though, a large server or a very important connection breaks. Then you might notice that a service you use suddenly stops working, or becomes very slow. Usually there are other servers offering the same service, so your computer can quietly switch to one of those — and things only 'stop working' for a short time.

But if lots of connections fail all at once, it can take many hours, or even days, to fix. Big failures are sometimes caused by a single connection breaking — if that connection is the only path to a server, then the data has no other route to take, and the service goes down completely.

There are many reasons a connection might break, and most of them happen close to home — in the connection between your own device and the internet. For example:

someone accidentally turns off the power;

someone unplugs a cable by mistake;

a fire damages the cables, or stops a server from working.

A helpful way to picture this is to imagine the internet as a set of roads connecting towns and cities. If there are roadworks or an accident on one road, drivers simply choose a different road. That other road might be narrower, so they cannot drive as fast — but they still get where they are going. The internet works in exactly the same way. When a connection breaks, data travels down other routes instead. Those routes get busier, so the data may travel more slowly. That is why, during a failure, you might notice pages take longer to load, or a video keeps stopping and starting.

concept-11-the-effects-of-network-failur.example: There is one more danger. Sometimes, during a network failure, data can become corrupted. This means the data is damaged so badly that it cannot be used — and it may be lost forever. That is why saving your work often, and keeping copies, is such a wise habit.

concept-12-how-companies-protect-against.explanation:
Because large networks — like those of banks, hospitals and big websites — are so important, companies spend a lot of money trying to stop them from failing. Their main trick is to avoid having only one of anything. A large failure is far more likely when there is only a single server, because if it breaks, there is nothing to take over.

So companies make copies of their servers, called backups. If one server breaks, a second, spare server takes over straight away, and users often do not notice anything at all. They also keep backup or 'spare' connections ready, so data always has another route. This idea — having spares ready so the system keeps working even when one part fails — is a hugely important idea in computing. You will use it yourself in your Final Project when you write a plan to keep Ehel Academy's network running.

Some of the biggest network failures in history hit gaming services like the PlayStation Network and Steam. Millions of gamers all around the world suddenly could not play the games they wanted to play — all at the same time! Even the largest companies are not completely safe from network failure.

"Give me a real-life situation where a network fails — like a video stopping, or a shop not being able to take payments. Ask me whether it is a small failure or a large failure, and ask me what could be done to prevent it. Then check my answer."

concept-13-staying-safe-and-responsible-.explanation:
Understanding how networks work also means understanding how to use them safely and kindly. You already value trust, honesty and respect, and you know that other people's privacy matters — and these same values make you a safe and responsible person online. Here is how to put them into practice:

Guard your private information. Never share your full name, home address, school, phone number or passwords with people you do not know online.

Only visit websites you trust. If you are not sure about a site, ask a teacher or a trusted adult before you visit it.

Use a strong password for your accounts, and never share it — not even with a friend. A network with no password lets strangers join, which is why Wi-Fi should always be protected.

Be trustworthy with other people's data. If a friend shares something private with you, keep it private. Do not spread other people's photos or messages without permission.

we01.solution:
Computers can only share files, printers and software if they are joined together into a network. Think of a network like a group of friends who can all talk to each other. On its own, one computer is like a person standing alone in a room. Connect it to a network and suddenly it can talk to every other device — sharing photos, sending messages, and reaching the whole internet.

There are two ways a device can join a network: with wires, or without wires (wirelessly). Both work well, but each needs different hardware. Hardware means the real, physical machines you could hold in your hand — as opposed to software, which is the programs that run on them. In this part you will meet three key pieces of network hardware.

Connecting with wires: the Ethernet cable

Many devices connect to a network using an Ethernet cable. It looks a little like a thick telephone wire with a clip on the end that clicks into a socket. Wired connections are fast and reliable, but the device cannot move far because it is tied to the cable. Two important devices use these cables to build a network: the switch and the router. They have lots of sockets, so many cables (and therefore many devices) can plug into them at once.

The switch — a meeting point for wired devices

A switch lets you connect wired devices together on one network, such as your school network or an office network. You can plug in many devices, for example:

The switch joins all these devices together so they can communicate — that is, send data to and receive data from each other. Here is the clever part: if you connect a single printer to the switch, then every computer on that network can use that one printer. The switch is like a busy meeting point where all the wired devices come together to talk. On its own, though, a switch cannot reach the internet — it only connects devices that are on the same network.

The router — the doorway to the internet

A router does something different. It lets different networks talk to each other. Its most common job is to connect a small network — like your home or school — to the huge network we call the internet.

For example, a router connects Ehel Academy's network to the internet. Because of the router, any device on the school network can reach the internet — so a student can open a website, watch a lesson video, or send a message to a cousin far away. If you remember only one thing, remember this: it is the router — and only the router — that lets devices on your network reach other networks and the internet.

Connecting without wires: the wireless access point

A wired switch and a wireless access point do a similar job — they both let computers join a network. The big difference is that the wireless access point needs no cables. Devices connect to it through the air. This is perfect for devices that move around, such as:

The most common wireless access point is a Wi-Fi access point. It sends and receives signals — special invisible waves that carry data through the air to and from nearby devices. A huge advantage is that hundreds of devices can connect to a single Wi-Fi access point without any wires at all. Compare that to a wired switch, which needs one separate cable for every single device!

Wi-Fi signals only travel a short distance, though. The further you walk away from the access point, the weaker the signal becomes — until, eventually, your device drops off the network. That is why Wi-Fi access points are often fixed high up on walls or ceilings, sometimes with an aerial sticking out. An aerial is the part that helps send and receive the signals.

How is a wireless access point different from a switch?

If you put a switch and a Wi-Fi access point side by side, the biggest difference is simple: the switch uses cables, while the wireless access point uses signals through the air. A switch is best for devices that stay still, like a desktop computer or a printer. A wireless access point is best for devices you carry around, like a phone or a tablet. Both connect devices to the same network — they just do it in different ways.

Here is how the three devices fit together in a typical network. Read the diagram below from top to bottom — the internet is at the top, and the devices are at the bottom:

A simple network: the router reaches the internet; the switch connects wired devices; the wireless access point connects devices with no wires.

+-----------+ +--------------------+

+-----------+ +--------------------+

In many homes there is just ONE box that plugs into the wall — people call it 'the Wi-Fi' or 'the router'. But that single box is actually doing three jobs at once! Inside it there is a router, a switch, AND a wireless access point, all built together. In a big school or office, these three are often separate machines so they can handle many more devices.

"Give me a device — like a printer, a phone or a smart TV — and ask me whether it would connect to the network through the switch, the wireless access point, or the router. Then tell me if I was right and explain why."

This turns your tutor into a quiz partner and helps the three devices stick in your memory.

For example: "A switch connects my computer to the internet." Not quite! A switch only connects devices to each other on the SAME network. To reach the internet, the data must go through the ROUTER. The switch is the meeting point inside your network; the router is the doorway out to the wider world.

we02.solution:
You now know the hardware that joins devices together. But how does a message actually travel from your device, across the world, and arrive at exactly the right computer? That is the amazing journey you will follow in this part.

Cellular networks: the internet almost anywhere

A cellular network is another kind of wireless network, but it works over very large areas. Instead of a small Wi-Fi box on a wall, cellular networks use tall towers (you may have seen them standing high above towns and along roads). These towers send out strong signals that a smartphone can pick up from many kilometres away.

A single cell tower can reach a phone up to about 50 kilometres away, although most of the time the useful range is around 5 kilometres. Making the towers tall is important, because it means the signal is less likely to be blocked by hills or buildings. This is why a mobile phone can connect almost anywhere — from the top of a mountain to the middle of a busy city. Some cars even use cellular networks, so they can download new software or let people make calls from inside the car.

Cellular networks have one big advantage: they cover enormous areas. But they share the same weakness as Wi-Fi — they can suffer from interference. Interference is anything that gets in the way of the signal, such as thick walls or bad weather. When there is interference, the signal may not reach your device properly. This can stop your phone from connecting, or make everything very slow.

For example: Fifty kilometres is a very long way. If you ran around a 400-metre running track, you would have to go around it about 125 times to run 50 km! That is roughly the furthest a single cell tower can send its signal.

we03.solution:
You have now met three ways for a device to connect: Wi-Fi, a wired Ethernet cable, and a cellular network (mobile data). Each one suits a different job. You would not want your phone tied to a wire while you walked around a city — and you would not use a slow, faraway cell tower to connect a printer that sits right next to your computer.

One way we compare connections is by their range — how far they reach. Another is their speed. Connection speed is measured in megabits per second, written Mbps. This is the fastest rate at which data can be sent. A higher number means data arrives more quickly, which matters a lot when you are streaming a video or downloading a big file.

IP addresses: every device has its own address

Think of the millions and millions of devices connected to the internet. When your device sends data, how does the internet know which of all those devices to deliver it to? The answer is that every device has its own unique address, called an IP address. IP stands for Internet Protocol.

An IP address is a set of numbers. A common type is made of four numbers separated by full stops, and each number is between 0 and 255. For example, a device might have the address 43.66.141.66. These numbers tell a computer exactly where to send data to, or where to fetch data from. IP addresses are usually created automatically by a small program, so you never have to type them yourself.

The best way to picture an IP address is to think of the address on a letter, or a post code. Every home has its own address so the postal worker knows exactly where to deliver each letter. In the same way, every device has its own IP address so the internet knows exactly where to deliver each piece of data. And just as no two homes on a street can share the same house number, no two devices on a network can share the same IP address — the automatic program makes sure each one is unique, so there is never any confusion.

There are two types of IP address. The older type is called IPv4 — and the world is starting to run OUT of IPv4 addresses, because there are so many devices! So a newer type was invented, called IPv6, which has an almost unlimited number of addresses — enough for every device for a very, very long time.

Here is one of the most surprising ideas about the internet. When you send a message or a photo, it does not travel as one big lump. Instead, before it is sent, the data is chopped up into many small chunks called packets. Packets are usually all about the same size.

Imagine Nadia in Hargeisa wants to send a message to Sami in Mogadishu. Her computer splits the message into, say, three packets. But each packet is not just a piece of the message — it also carries some extra labels. Every packet includes:

the IP address it was sent from (Nadia's device),

the IP address it is going to (Sami's device),

a packet number, so the pieces can be put back in the right order,

and, of course, a small piece of the actual message (the packet data).

Here is what one packet looks like inside. Notice the address labels at the top and the piece of data at the bottom:

One data packet. The 'sent from' and 'sent to' IP addresses are like the return address and destination address on an envelope.

+------------------------------------------+

+------------------------------------------+

For example: Why bother with the return address? Because if a packet gets lost on the way, the computer that was waiting for it knows exactly which device to ask to send it again. The labels make the whole system reliable.

we04.solution:
When Nadia's packets set off across the internet, something interesting happens: they may take different routes to reach Sami. Just like cars driving from one city to another can take different roads, packets can travel by different paths. Some routes are quicker than others, so the packets often arrive in the wrong order!

This is not a problem, thanks to the packet number. When the packets arrive at their destination, Sami's computer reads the numbers and uses them to put the packets back into the correct order — like sorting shuffled pages of a story back to 1, 2, 3. Only once all the packets have arrived and are in order can the computer read the full message. Here is the whole journey in four steps:

For example: The four steps of sending data: split, send, travel, reassemble.

What happens if a packet gets lost?

Sometimes a packet does not arrive at all — it gets lost along the way. When that happens, the internet has a neat way of fixing it:

The receiver computer notices a packet is missing, and sends a message back to the sender asking: "Please send packet 2 again, it got lost."

The sender computer sends another copy of just that one lost packet.

When the copy arrives, the receiver now has all the packets, so it puts them in order.

For example: The full message is complete, and the computer can finally use the data.

we06.solution:
Splitting data into packets is a clever idea, and it brings real benefits — but it also has a few costs. It is important to understand both sides.

If a packet is lost, only a small piece of data has to be sent again — not the whole message.

Packets do not take up much bandwidth each, so they can travel along a greater variety of connections.

For example: Smaller packets are less likely to get stuck or delayed on a busy network.

bug-1.fix: When something goes wrong, people often shout: “The internet is broken!” But remember: the internet itself does NOT break. It is far too big for that. What actually breaks is just the CONNECTIONS between some of the computers. There are almost always other connections the data can use instead. The effects of network failures Network failures can have very small effects, or very big effects. Small failures happen quite often, and they are usually just annoying rather than serious. For example, if a network fails while you are working online, any work you have not saved recently might disappear. Or if you are playing an online game, the game might suddenly stop. Frustrating — but not the end of the world. Large failures with big effects do not happen as often, but they matter far more. Imagine a bank's network failing. outcomes: An evaluation is much stronger when you have success criteria — a clear list of what the program should do to be a success. Without criteria, feedback is vague ('I liked it, but it was a bit small'). With criteria, feedback is useful. Compare these two evaluations of an animation:
Weak (no criteria): 'I really liked the animation. The polar bear did a backflip, but it was a bit small.'

Strong (with criteria): 'The sprites could be improved by making the polar bear bigger and the llama smaller. The text only showed for one second — it should stay for three or four seconds so the user can read it. I liked how a repeat loop was used for the backflip.'
The strong evaluation is better because it checks the program against clear criteria (sprite sizes, text timing, use of loops) and says exactly how to improve.

Everything the user sees and hears is the user experience (sometimes shortened to UX). It does not include the code, because users almost never see the code. Programmers think hard about UX: where the menus go, how the screen looks, which buttons show. Good UX makes a program a pleasure to use; bad UX makes it frustrating.

Systematic means careful and organised, following a sensible method — not just testing at random. To test the rock, paper, scissors game systematically, Zara tests it 15 times: five times entering 'rock', five times 'paper', and five times 'scissors'. Each time she records what happened. The more times a program works correctly, the more confident she can be that there are no bugs.
Here is the testing table she uses:

She also tests with unexpected data. What if the user types bananas, or a number, or a single letter? A well-made program should not crash — it should politely handle input it did not expect, for example by saying 'Please type rock, paper or scissors.' Thinking about unexpected data is a key part of good testing.
Improving code and software updates

Testing and evaluating never really stop. Have you noticed how apps and devices sometimes ask you to install an update? That is because teams of developers keep improving their programs even after they are released. They fix bugs they missed, and they add improvements to the user experience. When you accept an update, you get their newest and best version. It is always wise to install updates, because they often include security improvements that keep your device safe.

concept-1-planning-flowcharts.explanation:
Before a programmer writes any code, they usually make a plan. One of the best ways to plan is to draw a flowchart. A flowchart is a diagram that shows every step of an algorithm. An algorithm is just a set of step-by-step instructions — like a recipe, or the directions from your home to school.

You have already met algorithms in earlier years. In Scratch you build an algorithm out of blocks. You can also write an algorithm in words, or say it out loud. A flowchart is one more way to show the same idea, but as a picture. Pictures are easy to follow with your finger, and they help you spot mistakes before you start coding.

You always begin at the Start shape at the top. Then you follow the arrow to the next step, and the next, until you reach the End shape. Here is a simple flowchart for making breakfast, written as text so you can read it top to bottom:

A simple flowchart shown as text (each | is a connector arrow)

If you follow this with your finger, the result is clear: you end up eating breakfast. This flowchart uses sequence only — one step after another, always in the same order.

The shape of each box tells you what kind of step it is. This is important: the shape gives information all by itself. Here are the five shapes you must know.

The decision shape is the most powerful one. It works just like a conditional statement (IF ... THEN ... ELSE) in code. It asks a question that can only be answered Yes or No, and then the flowchart follows a different arrow depending on the answer.

Here is Maya's morning-routine flowchart. Notice the decision: 'Is it a school day?'. Depending on the answer, she takes out different clothes.

Is it a school day? --- No ---> Take out your weekend clothes

Let us predict the result. If it IS a school day, we follow the Yes arrow: we take out the school uniform, then eat breakfast, then finish. If it is NOT a school day, we follow the No arrow: we take out weekend clothes, then eat breakfast, then finish. Both paths join back together before breakfast. This is exactly how selection works in a real program.

So what is the big difference between the breakfast flowchart and this morning-routine flowchart? The breakfast flowchart has only ONE path — everybody follows the exact same steps in the exact same order. The morning-routine flowchart has TWO possible paths because of the decision diamond. Depending on the answer to the question, you take a different route. A flowchart with no decision does the same thing every single time; a flowchart with a decision can behave differently depending on the situation. That is what makes decisions so useful.

To predict means to say what you think will happen before it happens. To predict the outcome of a flowchart, you follow every step to the end. Here is a flowchart for fixing a computer that will not switch on:

Is the computer plugged into the mains? --- No ---> Plug the computer into the mains

Is the power cable plugged into the computer? --- No ---> Plug the power cable in

Predict the result if the computer is already plugged into the mains AND the cable is already plugged in: both decisions answer Yes, so we skip straight past both 'plug in' steps and reach the End. The prediction is: the computer should already be working, so we do not need to do anything. People use flowcharts like this in real life to predict things such as which patients might need certain healthcare, or whether the price of gold will rise or fall.

Engineers use flowcharts to show how to build machines, and businesses use them to explain how to do a job. A robot that plays chess can be programmed with a flowchart — if you understand the flowchart, you can predict its next move!

Shape name — What it looks like · What it means

Start or End — Oval (rounded) shape · Shows the very beginning and the very end of the flowchart.

Connector — Arrow · Shows the order to follow the steps in.

Input or Output — Parallelogram (leaning rectangle) · Getting information from the user, or giving information to the user.

Process — Rectangle · An action the program does, such as a calculation.

concept-4-data-types.explanation:
Computers organise data into data types. You need three of them in this unit.

Integer — a whole number, such as 3. The numbers 3.14 and the word 'three' are NOT integers. You can do maths with integers.

Character — a single letter, symbol or number, such as A, !, or 4. Your keyboard is full of characters. Strong passwords mix letters, symbols and numbers.

String — two or more characters joined together, such as a word or a sentence. Strings can include spaces and are used for messages. The Scratch say [ ] block needs a string.

In Scratch, if you type a string where only an integer is accepted, Scratch changes it to 0. That is why trying to add the words 'three' + 'five' gives 0 — you cannot add two words together like numbers!

concept-5-scratch-chatbot-using-string-a.explanation:
say (join [You are about ] (join ((current [year v]) — (birthYear)) [ years old!])) for 3 seconds

Trace the result. Suppose the user types Ben then 2015. The chatbot says 'Hello! My name is Robo.', then 'Nice to meet you, Ben', then it works out the age and says 'You are about 11 years old!'. Notice we use the current [year] block (the same clock block you met in the talking clock) instead of typing this year's number ourselves, so the age is always right — in 2026 the block gives 2026, so 2026 - 2015 = 11. The name is a string; the year is used as an integer in the subtraction; and join glues the pieces of the message together.

Chatbots are only programs following an algorithm, so their answers are not always reliable. Some hackers build chatbots to steal personal information. Only chat with a chatbot on a website or app you trust, and never share private details.

concept-6-sub.explanation:
A sub-routine is a section of code, separate from the main code, that does one specific job. The clever thing is that you can use it again and again. Programmers use sub-routines to make code easier to read and to avoid writing the same instructions many times.

There are two important words. To define a sub-routine means to give it a name and write all its instructions. To call a sub-routine means to use it — like calling a friend's name in the yard and they respond. You can call the same sub-routine many times, and different parts of your program can call it.

Imagine a gymnast's routine. A 'handstand' has four steps and a 'forward roll' has three steps. If you wrote out every step every time, the instructions would be enormous. Instead, you define each move once, then just call it:

Using sub-routines to keep a routine short

4 Put your feet back on the floor

See how short Routine 1 is? The same handstand and forward roll sub-routines could be used in a completely different Routine 2 as well. That is the power of sub-routines: define once, call anywhere.

A good quiz game usually needs two variables: one for the score and one for the lives. Here is the exact two-variable algorithm from your textbook, which we will use again in the quiz:

An algorithm that uses two variables

Trace the result. At the start, Score is 0 and Lives is 3 — this is called initialisation. If the player answers 7, the condition is true, so Score becomes 1 and Lives stays 3. If the player answers 5, the condition is false, so the ELSE branch runs: Lives becomes 2 and Score stays 0. To start with 5 lives, change set Lives to 3 into set Lives to 5. To give 2 points for a correct answer, change change Score by 1 into change Score by 2.

The same variable in two different sprites

The answer variable is shared, so two sprites can both use it. Leo makes a sprite that asks a question and a second sprite (Maya's sprite) that reacts to the same answer, using a broadcast to connect them:

Two sprites sharing the answer variable

Trace the result. If the user types basketball, Sprite 1 says 'I love basketball' and then broadcasts a message. Sprite 2 hears the message and says 'basketball is a great sport too!'. Both sprites used the SAME answer variable in their own separate scripts.

Sub-routines in Scratch: broadcast and receive

Scratch is a block-based language: you drag and drop blocks. To make a sub-routine in Scratch, you use the broadcast [ ] block to send a message, and a when I receive [ ] block to catch it and run the sub-routine. (There is also a 'Make a Block' button that does something similar, in a more powerful way.)

Here is Maya's spelling quiz. The user must spell the word 'variable'. Getting it right or wrong each calls a sub-routine:

Spelling quiz with two sub-routines

Trace the result. If the user types variable exactly, the correct sub-routine runs: a 'Tada' sound plays, the score goes up by 1, it says 'Correct!', and the backdrop changes to Party. If the user types anything else, the wrong sub-routine runs: a 'Clang' sound plays, a life is lost, it says 'Not quite...', and the backdrop turns red. Because these actions are in sub-routines, EVERY question can reuse them — you do not rewrite them for each question.

Initialisation means getting everything ready at the start of a program. In a car game, blocks like go to x: (-100) y: (110) and point in direction (90) reset the car to the same starting place every time the green flag is clicked. Here is a car game that uses a sub-routine called 'Off course!':

Car game with an 'Off course!' sub-routine and initialisation

--- Sub-routine: Off course! ---

Trace the result. The car starts at the same place each time (initialisation). The forever loop keeps checking: if the car touches the black edge of the track, it broadcasts 'Off course!'. The sub-routine then says 'Off course!' and puts the car back at the start. If you added a second car for a two-player game, it could call the SAME 'Off course!' sub-routine — no need to rewrite it. Two sprites that affect each other like this are said to interrelate.

There is one more big reason to love sub-routines: they make your programs much easier to test and fix. If the same actions were copied into ten different places and you found a mistake, you would have to fix it ten times — and you might miss one. With a sub-routine, that code lives in ONE place, so you fix the bug once and it is corrected everywhere the sub-routine is called. As your programs grow bigger, this becomes one of the most valuable skills you can have.

concept-8-interface-prompts-and-prototyp.explanation:
The interface is what the user sees on the screen: the sprites, the backdrops and the messages. A prompt is a message that shows the program is waiting for input, such as 'Type rock, paper or scissors'. Before building the whole game, programmers make a prototype — a basic first version that users can test and give feedback on. It is much easier to fix mistakes at the prototype stage.

People who work on how a program looks are called front-end developers. People who work on the code the user does not see are called back-end developers. Even famous game consoles like the Nintendo DS started life as a prototype!

Random means an outcome you cannot predict, like a dice roll. Scratch has a pick random ( ) to ( ) block. Prioritising means deciding what to build first — and it usually makes sense to build the hardest, most important parts first. Zara prioritises (1) the computer's random choice and (2) working out the winner.

Here is a common bug and its fix. Zara first wrote three separate IF blocks, each with its own pick random 1 to 3. Because a NEW random number was picked in each IF, the answers did not match up and sometimes nothing was said. The fix is to pick the random number ONCE and store it in a variable:
concept-8-interface-prompts-and-prototyp.example: Trace the result. The random number is chosen a single time and stored in computerChoice. Say it is 2; then computerWord is set to 'paper', and the sprite says 'I chose paper'. Because we stored the number, every IF checks the SAME value — the bug is gone.

Building a program is only half the job. Good programmers then evaluate and test their work. Evaluation means thinking about what you like, what you dislike, and how the program could be improved. It is one of the main ways we keep getting better.

An evaluation is much stronger when you have success criteria — a clear list of what the program should do to be a success. Without criteria, feedback is vague ('I liked it, but it was a bit small'). With criteria, feedback is useful. Compare these two evaluations of an animation:

Weak (no criteria): 'I really liked the animation. The polar bear did a backflip, but it was a bit small.'

Strong (with criteria): 'The sprites could be improved by making the polar bear bigger and the llama smaller. The text only showed for one second — it should stay for three or four seconds so the user can read it. I liked how a repeat loop was used for the backflip.'

The strong evaluation is better because it checks the program against clear criteria (sprite sizes, text timing, use of loops) and says exactly how to improve.

Improving code and software updates

Testing and evaluating never really stop. Have you noticed how apps and devices sometimes ask you to install an update? That is because teams of developers keep improving their programs even after they are released. They fix bugs they missed, and they add improvements to the user experience. When you accept an update, you get their newest and best version. It is always wise to install updates, because they often include security improvements that keep your device safe.

You can work the same way. When a classmate or your teacher finds something to improve in your program, do not feel bad — the biggest technology companies in the world improve their programs all the time. Make the change, then save your project with a note like 'version 2' or 'version 3', so you can see how your work has grown.

One famous online game was released before it had been properly tested. It was full of bugs, players around the world complained, the reviews were terrible, and the company had to give everyone their money back — losing millions. Testing matters!

concept-11-using-variables-with-a-physic.explanation:
Now for something different: a physical programming device — a small computer you can hold in your hand and program yourself. The one we use is the BBC micro:bit. It has inputs (buttons A and B, a microphone, sensors) and outputs (a grid of LED lights and a tiny speaker).

You do NOT need to own a micro:bit

Go to makecode.microbit.org (blocks) or python.microbit.org (Python). A picture of a micro:bit appears on the left of the screen. When you run your code, this simulator behaves exactly like a real micro:bit — you can click its buttons with your mouse. Everything in this unit can be done with the free online simulator alone.

Every computer, including the micro:bit, follows the IPO model: it takes in data (input), works on it (process), then gives data out (output). For example: you press buttons on a calculator (input), it works out the answer (process), and it shows the answer on the screen (output). All of this happens very quickly.

Long ago, computers filled whole rooms, but scientists made them smaller and smaller until the portable game console was born — a little computer you could carry outside and play games on. The micro:bit is like your very own tiny games console: once you download your game onto it and attach a battery pack, you can take your program out to the school yard, just like Sami wants to.

The first ever machine that could be called a computer was designed in 1837 by an English mathematician, Charles Babbage. He called it the Analytical Engine. Ada Lovelace, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, was one of the first people ever to write instructions for this machine — which makes her one of the first computer programmers in history!

Functions: sub-routines for the micro:bit

In Scratch you made sub-routines with broadcast. MakeCode has no broadcast block — instead you use a function. A function is a separate section of code that runs when it is called from the main code, and it can be called many times. It does exactly what a sub-routine does: it makes code clearer, reduces repetition, and makes bugs easier to fix (you only fix the function once).

Here is a simple MakeCode function example. Button A shows a heart; button B shows a duck:

The very same program can be written in MicroPython at python.microbit.org. This is real, text-based code that runs on the simulator:

Trace the result. The while True: loop runs forever. Each time around, it checks the buttons. If you click button A, the function show_heart() is called and a heart appears on the LED screen. If you click button B, show_duck() is called and a duck appears. Pressing the simulator's reset button starts it again.

Now for Sami's pocket game. The micro:bit shows a number from 1 to 9. The player guesses whether the NEXT number will be higher (press A) or lower (press B). A correct guess adds to the score; a wrong guess ends the streak. Here it is in MakeCode:

project.brief: This is your big project — it brings together everything from the whole unit. Working alone or with a partner, you will design, build, test and evaluate your own quiz game in Scratch. This is the perfect chance to build Maya's spelling quiz idea, or invent your own topic (times tables, capital cities, or world festivals from around the world).
steps: Complete these six steps in order. Each one uses a skill from a different subunit.
Write success criteria (from 1.5). List what your quiz must do — for example: a friendly greeting, at least five questions, a score variable, and a final score shown at the end.
Draw a flowchart (from 1.1). Show the algorithm for one question: ask, check the answer with a decision, then add a point or lose a life.
Create a project plan (from 1.4). Decompose the quiz into parts (welcome, questions, scoring, ending) and decide the order to build them.
Create a prototype (from 1.4). Build a simple first version — just the welcome screen and one working question — and test it.
Develop the program (from 1.2 and 1.3). Add the rest of the questions. Use variables for score and lives, and sub-routines for the 'correct' and 'wrong' actions so you do not repeat code.
Test and evaluate (from 1.5). Test systematically with right answers, wrong answers and unexpected input. Then evaluate against your success criteria and note what you would improve.

Ideas to make it special: different levels with different backdrops; questions that get harder as you progress; different reactions for right and wrong answers; a countdown timer; and sprite animations to celebrate a win.

concept-1-capturing-data.explanation:
Before you can manage data, you have to capture it — that is, collect it. And before you collect it, you have to plan. Good data managers never just grab numbers randomly; they think carefully about what they want to find out and how they will find it out. This is called a statistical investigation.

What is a statistical investigation?

A statistical investigation is the collection of data to help you answer a question. For example, Maya might want to find out the mean (average) number of goals her team scores in a month. She would look at each match, write down the goals, and then work out the mean. Or Sami might want to find out how many different birds visit the school garden in one hour — he would sit and count them. Both of these are statistical investigations, because both collect data to answer a clear question.

Not all data is the same. Knowing which type you are collecting helps you choose the right tool to collect it. There are three types you need to know.

Here is the key difference to remember. Discrete data is counted and is always a whole number — you cannot have half a person in a room. Continuous data is measured and can be any value at all, like a temperature of 24.5 degrees or a height of 1.42 metres. Because continuous data can be so precise, capturing it needs extra care — and that is exactly what Sami's weather investigation needs.

When you plan a statistical investigation, you should ask yourself six questions before you collect a single number. Answering them first saves you a lot of trouble later.

What do I want to find out? For example, 'How does the temperature in Mogadishu change during the week?'

What questions will help me find it out? Your questions must give you exactly the data you need.

Who or what will I ask or measure? Be specific. 'The temperature outside our classroom' is specific; 'the temperature' is not.

How will I collect the data? A questionnaire for opinions, a thermometer or data logger for temperature, and so on.

How will I analyse the data? Perhaps with a spreadsheet, and a chart to make patterns easy to see.

What tools will I use throughout? A data logger, a spreadsheet, a database, or a form — or a mixture.

There is a range of computing tools you can use to capture data. Choosing the right one depends on the type of data and how you want to collect it.

Data loggers — a device that uses sensors to record data over time, all by itself. A weather station that records the temperature and wind speed every hour is a data logger. Because it works on its own, it can be left in a hard-to-reach place, like a mountain top, for months. Data loggers are excellent for capturing continuous data.

Spreadsheets — such as LibreOffice Calc. A spreadsheet stores data in a neat grid and can do calculations and draw charts. It is perfect for recording readings and then analysing them.

Databases — such as LibreOffice Base. A database stores, organises and lets you search large amounts of organised data quickly.

Forms and questionnaires — a series of questions people fill in. A form can be on paper, in a word processor, or an online form. Forms are great for collecting answers from many people.

Every year there are between 12,000 and 14,000 earthquakes around the world.

concept-2-designing-a-form-to-collect-co.explanation:
Continuous data can be tricky to capture, because it can be any value and it often changes over time. If you design a form to collect it, you must think carefully about five things, or your data will be messy and hard to use.

Phrase your questions precisely. 'What was the temperature outside your classroom at 12:00 on Monday?' is precise. 'What is the temperature?' is not — it does not say where or when.

How often should data be entered? If you want a reading three times a day, say so, and leave space for three readings each day.

Over what period should data be entered? For a week? For a month? Make it clear and leave enough space.

What measurements will you use? Degrees Celsius? Millimetres of rainfall? Kilograms? State the unit so everyone answers the same way.

How precise should the data be? For example, you might ask for answers to one decimal place, like 24.5, not 24.5123.

When you make a form, you choose a question type for each question — the way the question is asked and answered. Different types suit different data.

Open text questions let people write their own answer, such as 'Why do you like reading?'. They are good for opinions, but people might answer in the wrong format. You can control this with validation rules, which only accept certain kinds of answer.

Multiple choice questions let people pick from a set of answers, such as 'What is your favourite colour?'. They are quick, but they are not good for continuous data, because you would need a choice for every possible value — which is impossible.

Ranking questions let people choose on a scale, such as 'Rate today's lunch from 1 to 5'. They are great for opinions, but they do not collect continuous or discrete data.
concept-2-designing-a-form-to-collect-co.example: So which question type is best for collecting continuous data like temperature or height? An open text question with validation rules — such as a box that only accepts a number to one decimal place. This gives the precise, numerical answer you need while stopping people from typing nonsense.

concept-3-hands.explanation:
You do not need an expensive online form to capture continuous data carefully. You can build a smart data-capture sheet in LibreOffice Calc, and use its validation rules to make sure only sensible answers are accepted. This is exactly what Sami needs for his Mogadishu weather investigation. Here is how the sheet is set out:

To stop anyone typing a word or a silly number into the rainfall column, Sami adds a validation rule. He selects the cells B2:B8, then opens the menu Data > Validity. On the Criteria tab he sets Allow to Decimal, the condition to between, a Minimum of 0 and a Maximum of 500. Now the cells will only accept a decimal number from 0 to 500 — a real rainfall reading. On the Error Alert tab he chooses the Stop action, so a wrong entry is refused with a friendly message.

For categorical data, like the type of weather, validation can give a drop-down list instead. Sami selects a column, opens Data > Validity, sets Allow to List, and types the choices Sunny, Cloudy, Rainy and Windy, one per line. Now that column shows a neat drop-down arrow, and no one can misspell 'Sunny' or invent a new category by accident. That is a validation rule doing its job.

Type of data — What it is · Examples · A · B

Categorical — Data that can be grouped into categories. It is usually an opinion, a description, or a range. · Favourite colour, type of pet, favourite lesson, age group 7-11. · Day · Rainfall (mm)

Discrete — Numerical data that can only be whole numbers. You often count it, and you cannot have half. · Number of learners in a class, number of customers, number of goals. · Saturday · 1.2

concept-4-creating-a-spreadsheet.explanation:
Now that you can capture data, it is time to organise and analyse it. The best tool for numerical data is a spreadsheet, and you will use LibreOffice Calc. A spreadsheet is far more than a place to store numbers — it is a powerful calculator that can work on thousands of numbers at once and never makes an arithmetic mistake.

A spreadsheet is a document split into a large grid. Each little box in the grid is called a cell. The cells are organised into rows, which go across, and columns, which go down. Each row has a unique number (1, 2, 3, ...) and each column has a unique letter (A, B, C, ...). 'Unique' means one of a kind — there is only one row 3 and only one column B, just as there is only one of you.

When you open LibreOffice Calc, look for these parts of the screen:

The Name Box at the top-left corner, which shows the reference of the cell you have selected.

The Input Line (the formula bar) next to it, where you can see and type what is inside a cell.

The sheet tabs at the bottom (Sheet1, Sheet2, ...). One file can hold many sheets.

The AutoSum button, marked with the Greek letter sigma, which quickly adds up a column or row for you.

Every cell has an address made of its column letter and its row number. This is called a cell reference. The letter tells you the column (how far across), and the number tells you the row (how far down). So the cell where column B meets row 3 has the cell reference B3.

Cell references are the secret to a spreadsheet's power. Instead of typing a number into a calculation, you type the cell reference where that number lives. Then, if you ever change the number in that cell, every calculation that uses it updates automatically. It is like magic, but it is really just clever organisation.

To make a calculation in a spreadsheet, you write a formula. A formula is an instruction to do a calculation, and it always begins with an equals sign =. The = tells LibreOffice Calc, 'Do not treat this as ordinary text — work this out for me.' Formulas combine cell references with arithmetic operators, the symbols we use for maths:

For example, =C3*D4 multiplies the value in cell C3 by the value in cell D4. If C3 holds 2 and D4 holds 4, the formula returns 8. One golden rule: always put a formula in a separate cell — not in either of the cells you are using in the calculation. You can type a formula straight into an empty cell, or click the cell and type into the Input Line at the top.

A function is a ready-made calculation that is already built into LibreOffice Calc. Each function has a name, and you 'call' it by that name. Functions save you from writing very long formulas. There are more than 500 functions in Calc, but in this unit you will focus on two: SUM and AVERAGE.

concept-6-total-sales-in-shillings.explanation:
Average price per item: in B11 type =AVERAGE(B2:B8) -> 8000

Let us check those by hand so you can see the software is right. The numbers sold are 15, 20, 8, 5, 6, 4 and 3, which add up to 61. The item totals in column D are 30000, 60000, 40000, 40000, 60000, 48000 and 48000, which add up to 326000 shillings. And the seven prices are 2000, 3000, 5000, 8000, 10000, 12000 and 16000, which add up to 56000; divide by 7 and you get an average price of 8000 shillings. Amara is delighted — what would have taken her an hour with a paper and pencil took LibreOffice Calc less than a second.

A modern LibreOffice Calc sheet has 1,048,576 rows and up to 16,384 columns.

That is more than 17 billion cells in a single sheet — far more than anyone could ever fill by hand.

Calc also has more than 500 built-in functions, each one a ready-made calculation waiting for you to use it.

Real spreadsheets often hold huge amounts of data. The skill of a good data manager is selecting just the pieces you need to answer a question. To select data for a calculation in LibreOffice Calc you can either type the cell references into your formula, or click and drag across the cells you want. When you drag, Calc fills the range into your formula for you.

Imagine Sami's weather sheet holds a whole month of readings: maximum temperature, minimum temperature, humidity and rainfall. To find the mean maximum temperature for the month, he selects only the maximum-temperature column and uses AVERAGE on it. He would not try to average the wind direction, because 'north' and 'east' are categorical words, not numbers — you cannot calculate a mean of them. Choosing the right data is just as important as choosing the right formula.

Numbers in a grid are useful, but a chart makes patterns jump out at you. To turn Amara's data into a chart in LibreOffice Calc:

Select the data you want to show. For a chart of each item's total, select the Item column and the Total column together (A1:A8 and D1:D8).

Open the menu Insert > Chart. The Chart Wizard appears.

Step 1 — Choose a Chart Type. Pick Column for tall bars, or Bar for sideways bars. Click Next.

Step 2 and 3 — Data Range and Data Series. Check that 'First row as label' and 'First column as label' are ticked, then click Next.

Step 4 — Chart Elements. Type a Title such as 'Shop sales this week', label the axes, and tick Display legend. Click Finish.

Click anywhere outside the chart to leave edit mode. Your chart is done!

Now anyone can see at a glance that the water bottle and the exercise book brought in the most money, while the pen brought in the least. That is the power of turning data into a picture.

Just as you planned your form in 2.1, you should plan a spreadsheet before you build it. Ask yourself: What data will I use? What headings will the columns have? How will I organise it so it is easy to understand? What format will the data be in? What calculations do I want to do, and which formulas or functions will do them? A few minutes of planning saves a lot of tidying up later.

concept-7-creating-a-database.explanation:
A spreadsheet is wonderful for calculations. But when you want to store, organise and search a lot of information — like every book in the school library — a database is even better. In this subunit you will design a database, build it in LibreOffice Base, and learn to search it in seconds. This is exactly what the librarian, Nadia, needs.

A database is an organised set of data. It is useful because organised data is so much easier to use than a messy pile. A database is made up of records and fields.

A record is all the data about one thing. In a library database, one book is one record.

A field is a category of data within a record. For a book, the fields might be Title, Author, Category and Year.

An attribute is the actual piece of data in one field of one record — for example, the Title attribute of one particular book might be 'Somali Folk Tales'.

In a database, records are usually shown as rows and fields as columns — just like a spreadsheet grid. A record is complete when every field is filled in. Here is Nadia's library database, with six book records:

Look at record number 4. Its fields are BookID, Title, Author, Category, Year and 'On loan?'. Its attributes are 4, 'Somali Folk Tales', 'Dina Ali', 'Story', 2018 and 'No'. If Nadia wanted to know who wrote 'Somali Folk Tales', she would look at the Author field of that record and find the attribute 'Dina Ali'.

Every field stores a particular kind, or type, of data. Choosing the right data type keeps your database tidy and correct. Here are the main types you need to know.

For example, think of a record about a country: Country: Oman (a string of text), Size: 309500 km2 (an integer), Population: 4576298 (an integer), Language: Arabic (text), Currency: Omani rial (a string). In Nadia's library database, the BookID and Year fields are integers, the Title, Author and Category fields are text, and the 'On loan?' field is a special Yes/No type.

Sometimes we want data to *look* a certain way. Formatting controls how the data is displayed — without changing the real value underneath. In LibreOffice you format cells by selecting them and opening Format > Cells (the shortcut is Ctrl+1). Then you pick a category:
